<issue_description>
Incorrect handling of ! in string parse
Hello,

first of all, thanks for recently updating the project! Good to see that it is still being maintained!

I would like to report an issue that we saw using the parse function of the library. It appears that the handling of a ! in an attributeValue is incorrect, resulting in ldap string parser to raise an exception. This also happens with ldap search strings that have been generated by the library itself.

To demonstrate I have written the following test script where I create ldap strings using your library, and then immediately parse it again:

```
from ldap_filter import Filter

testcases =[
    "Test",
    "Test!",
    "Test(",
    "Test)",
    "Test(()",
    "Test(Admin!)",
    "Test(with_a_*)",
    "Test(with_a_:)",
    "Test(with_a_&)",
    "Test(with_a_|)",
    "Test(with_a_~)"

]

for value in testcases:
    output = Filter.AND([
        Filter.attribute('name').equal_to(value),
        Filter.attribute('mail').ends_with('@example.com'),
        Filter.OR([
            Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('accounting'),
            Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('operations')
        ])
    ])

    # Creation
    print(f"Testcase: {value}")
    print(f"String  : {output.to_string()}")

    # Parsing
    parsed = Filter.parse(output.to_string())
    attributeValue = parsed.filters[0].val
    print(f"Attribute: {attributeValue}")
    assert value == attributeValue
```

This results in:

```
Testcase: Test
String  : (&(name=Test)(mail=*@example.com)(|(dept=accounting)(dept=operations)))
Attribute: Test
Testcase: Test!
String  : (&(name=Test!)(mail=*@example.com)(|(dept=accounting)(dept=operations)))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/usr/test.py", line 33, in <module>
    parsed = Filter.parse(output.to_string())
  File "/home/usr/src/python-ldap-filter/ldap_filter/filter.py", line 48, in parse
    return parser.parse(filt, actions=ParserActions())
  File "/home/usr/src/python-ldap-filter/ldap_filter/parser.py", line 1530, in parse
    return parser.parse()
  File "/home/usr/src/python-ldap-filter/ldap_filter/parser.py", line 1513, in parse
    raise ParseError(format_error(self._input, self._failure, self._expected))
ldap_filter.parser.ParseError: Line 1: expected '\\', [^!*\x29], '*', ')'
(&(name=Test!)(mail=*@example.com)(|(dept=accounting)(dept=operations)))

```

I believe the problem is that the `!` is incorrectly excluded as a valid token for the value.

If I apply the following patch:
```
diff --git a/ldap_filter/parser.py b/ldap_filter/parser.py
index 12b38f7..3cc2cc5 100644
--- a/ldap_filter/parser.py
+++ b/ldap_filter/parser.py
@@ -142,7 +142,7 @@ class Grammar(object):
     _input_size = None
     _actions = None
 
-    REGEX_1 = re.compile('^[^!*\\x29]')
+    REGEX_1 = re.compile('^[^*\\x29]')
     REGEX_2 = re.compile('^[a-fA-F0-9]')
     REGEX_3 = re.compile('^[\\x20]')
     REGEX_4 = re.compile('^[\\x09]')
```

All strings are parsed correctly.

I am interested to hear what you think of this issue and if my fix is correct. I have looked at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4515#section-3 and saw that exclamation mark is not a character that requires escaping.

</issue_description>

   141	The `Filter.simplify()` method can be used to eliminate unnecessary AND/OR filters that only have one child node.
   142	
   143	``` python
   144	input = '(&(name=bob))'
   145	complex = Filter.parse(input)
   146	
   147	print(complex.simplify())  # (name=bob)
   148	```
   149	
   150	## Filter Output ##
   151	
   152	There are a few options for getting a string output from your `Filter` object with optional custom formatting.
   153	
   154	### Simple String ###
   155	
   156	You can get simple filter string by calling the `Filter.to_string()` method. The `Filter` class also implements Python's `__str__` method, allowing you to type cast the `Filter` object directly to a string or concatenate with other strings.
   157	
   158	``` python
   159	output = Filter.AND([
   160	    Filter.attribute('name').equal_to('bob'),
   161	    Filter.attribute('mail').ends_with('@example.com'),
   162	])
   163	
   164	# Filter.to_string() output.
   165	print(output.to_string())  # (&(name=bob)(mail=*@example.com))
   166	
   167	# Typecast output.
   168	print(str(output)) # (&(name=bob)(mail=*@example.com))
   169	
   170	# String concatenate output
   171	print('LDAP Filter: ' + output) # LDAP Filter: (&(name=bob)(mail=*@example.com))
   172	```
   173	
   174	### Beautified String ###
   175	
   176	The `Filter.to_string()` method provides additional formatting options to produce beautified filter strings.
   177	
   178	You can get the default beautified format by passing `True` to the `Filter.to_string(indent)` method

   181	output = Filter.AND([
   182	    Filter.attribute('name').equal_to('bob'),
   183	    Filter.attribute('mail').ends_with('@example.com'),
   184	    Filter.OR([
   185	        Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('accounting'),
   186	        Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('operations')
   187	    ])
   188	])
   189	
   190	print(output.to_string(True))
   191	```

   194	
   195	```
   196	(&
   197	    (name=bob)
   198	    (mail=*@example.com)
   199	    (|
   200	        (dept=accounting)
   201	        (dept=operations)
   202	    )
   203	)
   204	```
   205	
   206	or you can customize the output by passing the `indent` and/or `indt_char` parameters to `Filter.to_string(indent, indt_char)`. The `indent` parameter accepts an integer value while the `indt_char` parameter accepts any string or character value.
   207	
   208	``` python
   209	output = Filter.AND([
   210	    Filter.attribute('name').equal_to('bob'),
   211	    Filter.attribute('mail').ends_with('@example.com'),
   212	    Filter.OR([
   213	        Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('accounting'),
   214	        Filter.attribute('dept').equal_to('operations')
   215	    ])
   216	])
   217	
   218	print(output.to_string(2, '.'))
   219	```
   220

   223	```

   225	..(name=bob)
   226	..(mail=*@example.com)
   227	..(|
   228	....(dept=accounting)
   229	....(dept=operations)
   230	..)
   231	)
   232	```

   235	
   236	The `Filter.match(data)` method allows you to evaluate a Python dictionary with attributes against an LDAP filter. The method will return `True` if a match is found or `False` if there is no match (or if an attribute matches a **NOT** exclusion).

   241	    Filter.NOT(
   242	        Filter.attribute('status').equal_to('terminated')

    28	Introduction
    29	============
    30	
    31	estimagic is a Python package that provides high-quality and user-friendly tools
    32	to fit large scale empirical models to data and make inferences about the estimated
    33	model parameters. It is especially suited to solve difficult constrained optimization
    34	problems.
    35	
    36	estimagic provides several advantages over similar packages, including a unified
    37	interface that supports a large number of local and global optimization algorithms
    38	and the possibility of monitoring the optimization procedure via a beautiful
    39	interactive dashboard.
    40	
    41	estimagic provides tools for nonlinear optimization, numerical differentiation
    42	and statistical inference.
    43	
    44	
    45	Optimization
    46	------------
    47	
    48	- estimagic wraps all algorithms from *scipy.optimize* and many more become
    49	  available when installing optional dependencies.
    50	- estimagic can automatically implement many types of constraints via
    51	  reparametrization, with any optmizer that supports simple box constraints.
    52	- estimagic encourages name-based parameters handling. Parameters are specified
    53	  as pandas DataFrames that can have any kind of single or MultiIndex. This is
    54	  especially useful when specifying constraints.
    55	- The complete history of parameters and function evaluations are saved in a
    56	  database for maximum reproducibility and displayed in real time via an
    57	  interactive dashboard.
    58	
    59	
    60	.. image:: docs/source/_static/images/dashboard.gif
    61	  :scale: 21 %
    62	
    63	
    64	Numerical differentiation
    65	-------------------------
    66	
    67	- estimagic can calculate precise numerical derivatives using `Richardson extrapolations
    68	  <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson_extrapolation>`_.
    69	- Function evaluations needed for numerical derivatives can be done in parallel
    70	  with pre-implemented or user provided batch evaluators.
    71	
    72	
    73	Statistical Inference
    74	---------------------
    75	
    76	- estimagic provides asymptotic standard errors for maximum likelihood and method
    77	  of simulated moments.
    78	- estimagic also provides bootstrap confidence intervals and standard errors.
    79	  Of course the bootstrap procedures are parallelized.
    80	
    81	
    82	Installation
    83	============
    84	
    85	The package can be installed via conda. To do so, type the following commands in a
    86	terminal:
    87	
    88	.. code-block:: bash
    89	
    90	    $ conda config --add channels conda-forge
    91	    $ conda install -c opensourceeconomics estimagic
    92	
    93	The first line adds conda-forge to your conda channels. This is necessary for conda to
    94	find all dependencies of estimagic. The second line installs estimagic and its
    95	dependencies.

out_file = File(

Referencing the docs, I think this is an appropriate change:
> `hash_files`
To be used with inputs that are defining output filenames. When this flag is set to false any Nipype will not try to hash any files described by this input. This is useful to avoid rerunning when the specified output file already exists and has changed.

def _gen_filename(self, name): # this gets called when `out_file` is not defined

<issue_description>
The `extract_location` preprocessor doesn't work at the Met Office :(
**Describe the bug**

A new ESMValTool user at the Met Office was following the [quick start guide](https://esmvalgroup.github.io/ESMValTool_Tutorial/01-quickstart/index.html) and using our new ESMValTool v2.8.0 environment, but the recipe raised the exception:
```
geopy.exc.GeocoderUnavailable: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='nominatim.openstreetmap.org', port=443):
Max retries exceeded with url: /search?q=Amsterdam&format=json&limit=1 
(Caused by SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: 
self-signed certificate in certificate chain (_ssl.c:997)')))
```
The recipe works fine with our ESMValTool v2.7.0 environment.

I have been investigating this for a while; here are the key points:

+ I did not see any problems when running this recipe on JASMIN.
+ In ESMValTool v2.8.0, the [esmvaltool/recipes/examples/recipe_python.yml](https://github.com/ESMValGroup/ESMValTool/compare/v2.7.0...v2.8.0#diff-9ede07c7320e4272382fe41064146c3f8583e358e1cd14e5aaa67a7884c8047d) recipe was updated to use the `extract_location` preprocessor.
+ The `extract_location` preprocessor is (as far as I can tell) the only function in the entire code base that uses `geopy`.
+ I can reproduce the problem by running the code [within the `extract_location` function](https://github.com/ESMValGroup/ESMValCore/blob/9406b7eb7828a8d1a1328697158e4e7805b0a3c6/esmvalcore/preprocessor/_regrid.py#L363) in an interactive Python session:
```
% python
Python 3.10.10 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Mar 24 2023, 20:08:06) [GCC 11.3.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> from geopy.geocoders import Nominatim
>>> geolocator = Nominatim(user_agent="test_emma")
>>> geolocation = geolocator.geocode("Amsterdam")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  [...]
geopy.exc.GeocoderUnavailable: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='nominatim.openstreetmap.org', port=443):
Max retries exceeded with url: /search?q=Amsterdam&format=json&limit=1
(Caused by SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed:
self-signed certificate in certificate chain (_ssl.c:997)')))
```
+ The problem ultimately is the fault of `geopy`, since  [`requests.Session().trust_env` is hard-coded in `geopy` to be equal to `False`](https://github.com/geopy/geopy/blob/2.3.0/geopy/adapters.py#L397), which prevents our SSL certificates from being used (see [Requests Documentation: trust_env](https://docs.python-requests.org/en/latest/api/#requests.Session.trust_env) for slightly more information). 
+ This can be overridden as follows:
```
% python
Python 3.10.10 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Mar 24 2023, 20:08:06) [GCC 11.3.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> from geopy.geocoders import Nominatim
>>> import ssl
>>> ssl_context = ssl.create_default_context()
>>> geolocator = Nominatim(user_agent="test_emma", ssl_context=ssl_context)
>>> geolocation = geolocator.geocode("Amsterdam")
>>> print(geolocation)
Amsterdam, Noord-Holland, Nederland
>>> 
```
Would it be possible to implement this in ESMValCore, please? I'm not sure whether [ssl.create_default_context()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#ssl.create_default_context) would cause issues for others (I can't think of a reason why it would?), but I would be happy to create a PR for testing purposes?

<issue_description>
BUG: `Worksheet.isSheetHidden` is not updated when `Worksheet.hide()` or `Worksheet.show()` used
**Describe the bug**
[`Worksheet.isSheetHidden`] is not updated when [`Worksheet.hide`] or [`Worksheet.show`] (i.e., [`Worksheet._set_hidden_flag`]) is used.

**To Reproduce**

Create a spreadsheet with **minimum 2** worksheets.

```python
import gspread

gc = gspread.service_account(filename="./creds.json")
spreadsheet = gc.open("gspread test spreadsheet")
sheet = spreadsheet.sheet1

print("Sheet hidden (true/false):)")
print("initial:", sheet.isSheetHidden)

spreadsheet.worksheets()[1].hide()
print("after hide:", sheet.isSheetHidden)

spreadsheet.worksheets()[1].show()
print("after show:", sheet.isSheetHidden)
```

**Expected behavior**
```text
Sheet hidden (true/false):)
initial: False
after hide: True
after show: False
```

**Actual behavior**
```text
Sheet hidden (true/false):)
initial: False
after hide: False
after show: False
```

**Environment info:**
- Operating System: Windows
- Python version: 3.11.0
- gspread version: v5.9.0

**Additional context**
[`Worksheet._properties`] is set only when `Worksheet` is initialised.

Thus, whenever a property is changed, the correct API request must be sent, and then the property must be manually updated. For example, [`Worksheet.update_title`] runs [`self._properties[["title"]] = title`](https://github.com/burnash/gspread/blob/28e733fff2cf7f642c53a029389ad5b4516c8ec3/gspread/worksheet.py#L1405):

```python
    def update_title(self, title):
        ...
        body = {
            ...
        }

        response = self.spreadsheet.batch_update(body)
        self._properties["title"] = title
        return response
```

## Internal behavior comparison

I had a look to see which "meta field updaters" remember (or don't!) to update the internal `Worksheet._properties` object with the update.

I call a "meta field updater" anything that updates things about the spreadsheet that are not the cells, i.e., name, tab color, etc. (i.e., spreadsheet properties). They can be found by searching for requests which send an `"updateSheetProperties"` request.

*This is not an exhaustive list*

### meta field updaters which *do* change `Worksheet._properties`

- [`Worksheet.update_title`]
- [`Worksheet.update_tab_color`]

### meta field updaters which *do not* change `Worksheet._properties`

- [`Worksheet.resize`]
- [`Worksheet.update_index`]
- [`Worksheet.freeze`]
- [`Worksheet._set_hidden_flag`] (and thus [`Worksheet.hide`] & [`Worksheet.show`])

Thus, this is why the bug exists. In fixing this, it is probably worth fixing all 4 of these at once.

   179	Why grappa?
   180	-----------
   181	
   182	``grappa`` aims to assist humans while doing a very recurrent and not very fun task in software development: testing things.
   183	
   184	The core idea behind ``grappa`` comes from the fact that human time is considerably more expensive than machine time,
   185	and therefore any machine assistance to optimize processes and close the gap is beneficial.
   186	
   187	With ``grappa`` you can express almost in plain English what the test contract actually is, but in a way that's
   188	fun and easy to write but also more easy and pleasant to read or maintain by other developers.
   189	
   190	
   191	The Zen of grappa
   192	-----------------
   193	
   194	- Testing is about feedback: detailed, easy to understand, human-friendly is always better.
   195	- Frictionless testing: introducing self-declarative behavior testing patterns can make testing more fun for test writers and more enjoyable for test readers.
   196	- Expressivity is paramount: humans should easily understand what the code is doing.
   197	- Human time is expensive: any modern software should assist people to identify and understand errors easily.
   198	- Make error reporting great again: feedback during testing is key, let's make it more handy and less frustrating.
   199	- Testing patterns consolidation: software expectations are limited to the boundaries of language data types and structures.
   200	- Hurt less feelings: seeing errors is not a nice thing, but it can be painless if details are showed you in a more gentle way.
   201	
   202	
   203	Features
   204	--------
   205	
   206	-  Behavior-oriented expressive fluent API.
   207	-  Built-in assertion DSL with English lexicon and semantics.
   208	-  Supports both ``expect`` and ``should`` assertion styles.
   209	-  Full-featured built-in `assertion operators`_.
   210	-  Human-friendly and detailed `error reporting`_.
   211	-  Built-in expectations difference comparison between subject and expected values.
   212	-  Extensible assertions supporting third-party `plugins`_.
   213	-  Assertion chaining and composition.
   214	-  Composable assertion via logical operators such as ``and`` & ``or``.
   215	-  Testing framework agnostic. Works with ``unittest``, ``nosetests``, ``pytest``, ``behave`` ...
   216	-  Easy to hack via programmatic API.
   217	-  Lightweight and (almost) dependency-free.
   218	-  Works with Python 2.7+, 3+, PyPy and potentially with other Python implementations.
   219	
   220	
   221	Installation
   222	------------
   223

    42	The simplest Specs are based on common predicate functions, such as
    43	``lambda x: isinstance(x, str)`` which asks "Is the object x an instance of ``str``?".
    44	Fortunately, Specs are not limited to being created from single predicates. Specs can
    45	also be created from groups of predicates, composed in a variety of useful ways, and
    46	even defined for complex data structures. Because Specs are ultimately backed by
    47	pure Python code, any question that you can answer about your data in code can be
    48	encoded in a Spec.
    49	
    50	Features
    51	--------
    52	
    53	* Simple API using primarily native Python types and data structures
    54	
    55	* Stateless, immutable Spec objects are designed to be created once, reused, and composed
    56	
    57	* Rich error objects point to the exact location of the error in the input value
    58	
    59	* Builtin factories for many common validations
    60	
    61	Installation
    62	------------
    63	
    64	Dataspec is developed on `GitHub <https://github.com/coverahealth/dataspec>`_ and hosted
    65	on `PyPI <https://pypi.org/project/dataspec/>`_. You can fetch Dataspec using ``pip``:
    66	
    67	.. code-block:: bash
    68	
    69	   pip install dataspec
    70	
    71	To enable support for phone number specs or arbitrary date strings, you can choose the
    72	extras when you install:
    73	
    74	.. code-block:: bash
    75	
    76	   pip install dataspec[dates]
    77	   pip install dataspec[phonenumbers]
    78	
    79	Getting Started
    80	---------------
    81	
    82	To begin using the ``dataspec`` library, you can simply import the ``s`` object:
    83	
    84	.. code-block:: python
    85	
    86	   from dataspec import s
    87	
    88	``s`` is a generic constructor for creating new Specs. Many useful Specs can be
    89	composed from basic Python objects like types, functions, and data structures. The
    90	"Hello, world!" equivalent for creating new Specs might be a simple Spec that validates
    91	that an input is a string (a Python ``str`` ). We can do this by simply passing the
    92	Python ``str`` type directly to ``s``. When ``s`` receives an instance of a ``type``
    93	object, it assumes you want to create a Spec that validates input values are of that
    94	type:
    95	
    96	.. code-block:: python
    97	
    98	   spec = s(str)
    99	   spec.is_valid("a string")  # True
   100	   spec.is_valid(3)           # False
   101	
   102	Often you want to assert more than one condition on an input value. After all, it's
   103	fairly trivial to assert type checks on a value. In fact, this may even be done by
   104	a deserialization library on your behalf. Perhaps you're interested in checking that
   105	your input is a string and that it contains only numbers and hyphens. ``dataspec`` lets
   106	you define Specs with boolean logic, which can be useful for asserting multiple
   107	conditions on your input:
   108	
   109	.. code-block:: python
   110	
   111	   spec = s.all(str, lambda s: all(c.isdecimal() or c == "-" for c in s))
   112	   spec.is_valid("212-867-5309")     # True
   113	   spec.is_valid("Philip Jennings")  # False
   114	
   115	Composition is at the heart of ``dataspec`` 's design. In the previous example, we
   116	learned a few useful things. First, ``s`` is actually a callable object with static
   117	methods which help produce other sorts of Specs. Second, we can see that when we
   118	pass objects understood to ``s`` into various Spec constructors, they are automatically
   119	coerced into the appropriate Spec type. Here, we passed a ``type``, which we used
   120	previously. We also passed in a function of one argument returning a boolean; in
   121	``dataspec``, these are called predicates and they are turned into Specs which validate
   122	input values if the function returns ``True`` and fail otherwise. Finally, we learned
   123	that ``s.all`` can be used to produce ``and`` -type boolean logic between different
   124	Specs. (You can produce ``or`` Specs using ``s.any``).
   125	
   126	In the previous example, we used the ``and`` logic to check for our conditions to show
   127	various different features of ``dataspec``. However, in real code you'd likely take
   128	advantage of ``dataspec`` 's builtin ``s.str`` factory, which can assert several useful
   129	properties of strings (in addition to the basic ``isinstance`` check). In the case
   130	above, perhaps we really wanted to check for a US ZIP code (with the trailing 4 digits).
   131	We can perform that check using a simple regex string validator:
   132	
   133	.. code-block:: python
   134	
   135	   spec = s.str("us_zip_plus_4", regex=r"\d{5}\-\d{4}")
   136	   spec.is_valid("10001-3093")  # True
   137	   spec.is_valid("10001")       # False
   138	   spec.is_valid("N0L 1E0")     # False
   139	
   140	Scalar Specs like the one above are trivially different from the same checks you could
   141	write in raw Python. The real power of ``dataspec`` comes from its ability to compose
   142	Specs for larger, nested data structures. Suppose you were accepting a physician
   143	profile object via a JSON API and you wanted to validate that the physician licenses
   144	were valid in all of the states you operate in:
   145	
   146	.. code-block:: python
   147	
   148	   operating_states = s("operating_states", {"CA", "GA", "NY"})
   149	   license_states = s("license_states", [operating_states, {"kind": list}])
   150	   license_states.is_valid(["CA", "NY"])  # True
   151	   license_states.is_valid(["SD", "GA"])  # False, you do not operate in South Dakota
   152	   license_states.is_valid({"CA"})        # False, as the input collection is a set
   153	
   154	In the previous example, we learned a bit more about ``dataspec``. First, we can see
   155	that Spec objects are designed to be reused. We declared ``operating_states`` as a
   156	separate Spec from ``license_states`` with the intent that we could use it as a
   157	component of other Specs. Specs are immutable and stateless, so they can be reused in
   158	other Specs without issue. Next, we can see that we're expecting a collection, indicated
   159	by the Python ``list`` wrapping ``operating_states`` in the ``license_states`` Spec.
   160	In particular, we are expecting exactly a ``list``, not a ``set`` or ``tuple``.
   161	Third, we are expecting a limited set of enumerated values, indicated by
   162	``operating_states`` being a ``set``. Values not in the set are rejected. ``dataspec``
   163	also supports using Python's ``Enum`` objects for defining enumerated types.
   164	
   165	We did declare two separate Specs and pass both to ``s`` directly. However, we could
   166	have declared the entire Spec inline and ``s`` would have converted each child value
   167	into a Spec automatically: ``s([{"CA", "GA", "NY"}, {"kind": list}])`` .
   168	
   169	Building on the previous example, let's suppose we want to validate a simplified
   170	version of that physician profile object. Spec is great for validating data at your
   171	application boundaries. You can pass it your deserialized input values and it will
   172	help you ensure that you're receiving data in the shape your internal services
   173	expect:
   174	
   175	.. code-block:: python
   176	
   177	   spec = s(
   178	       "user-profile",
   179	       {
   180	           "id": s.str("id", format_="uuid"),
   181	           "first_name": s.str("first_name"),
   182	           "last_name": s.str("last_name"),
   183	           "date_of_birth": s.str("date_of_birth", format_="iso-date"),
   184	           s.opt("gender"): s("gender", {"M", "F"}),
   185	           "license_states": license_states,  # using the previously defined Spec
   186	       }
   187	   )
   188	   spec.is_valid(  # True
   189	       {
   190	           "id": "e1bc9fb2-a4d3-4683-bfef-3acc61b0edcc",
   191	           "first_name": "Carl",
   192	           "last_name": "Sagan",
   193	           "date_of_birth": "1996-12-20",
   194	           "license_states": ["CA"],
   195	       }
   196	   )
   197	   spec.is_valid(  # False; the optional "gender" key included an invalid value
   198	       {
   199	           "id": "e1bc9fb2-a4d3-4683-bfef-3acc61b0edcc",
   200	           "first_name": "Carl",
   201	           "last_name": "Sagan",
   202	           "date_of_birth": "1996-12-20",
   203	           "gender": "O",
   204	           "license_states": ["CA"],
   205	       }
   206	   )
   207	   spec.is_valid(  # True; note that extra keys _are ignored_
   208	       {
   209	           "id": "958e2f55-5fdf-4b84-a522-a0765299ba4b",
   210	           "first_name": "Marie",
   211	           "last_name": "Curie",
   212	           "date_of_birth": "1867-11-07",
   213	           "gender": "F",
   214	           "license_states": ["NY", "GA"],
   215	           "occupation": "Chemist",
   216	       }
   217	   )
   218	   spec.is_valid(  # False; the "license_states" includes the invalid value "TX"
   219	       {
   220	           "id": "958e2f55-5fdf-4b84-a522-a0765299ba4b",
   221	           "first_name": "Marie",
   222	           "last_name": "Curie",
   223	           "date_of_birth": "1867-11-07",
   224	           "license_states": ["TX"],
   225	       }
   226	   )
   227	
   228	``dataspec`` includes plenty of additional functionality which is not discussed above.
   229	Read more at `Read the Docs <https://dataspec.readthedocs.io>`_.
   230	
   231	Why not X?
   232	----------
   233	
   234	Python's ecosystem features a rich collection of data validation and normalization
   235	tools, so a new entrant in the space naturally begs the question "why didn't you just
   236	use X instead?". Before creating Dataspec, we surveyed a wide variety of different
   237	tools and had even used one or two in our production service. All of these tools are
   238	generally successful at validating data, but each had some issue that caused us to
   239	pass.
   240	
   241	* Many of the libraries in this space primarily help validate data, but do not always
   242	  help you normalize or conform that data after it has been validated. Dataspec
   243	  provides validation and conformation out of the box.
   244	
   245	* Libraries which do feature validation and normalization often complect these two
   246	  steps. Dataspec validation is a discrete step that occurs before conformation, so
   247	  it is easy to reason about failures in validation.
   248	
   249	* Some of the libraries we tried were stateful or leaned too heavily on mutability.
   250	  We tend to prefer immutable and stateless objects where mutability and state is not
   251	  required. Specs in Dataspec are completely stateless and conformation always produces
   252	  a new value. This is certainly more costly than mutating inputs, but mutating code
   253	  is harder to reason about and is a major source of bugs, so we prefer to avoid it.
   254	
   255	* Many libraries we surveyed focused on defining validations from the top-down, rather
   256	  than encouraging composition. Specs in Dataspec are designed to be created once,
   257	  reused, and composed, rather than requiring a separate definition for each usage.
   258	
   259	License
   260	-------

```
Namespace(_=False, cfg_overrides=None, change_path=None, common_debug=False, common_idebug=False, common_on_failure=None, common_output_format='default', common_report_status=None, common_report_type=None, common_run_after=None, common_run_before=None, func=<bound method Interface.call_from_parser of <class 'datalad.interface.posarg.Posarg'>>, help=None, log_level='warning', logger=<logging.Logger object at 0x7f07c37babe0>, opt_arg=None, pbs_runner=None, pos-arg='ok', subparser=ArgumentParser(prog='datalad posarg', usage=None, description='Blah', formatter_class=<class 'argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter'>, conflict_handler='error', add_help=False))
```

Note the "pos-arg".  So, when `base.Interface.call_from_parser` [goes looking][1] for `pos_arg`, it doesn't find it, leading to the attribute error.

Or, to remove this from the context of datalad:

```python
>>> import argparse
>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
>>> parser.add_argument('fo-o')
>>> parser.add_argument('--ba-z')
>>> parser.parse_args('arg'.split())
Namespace(ba_z=None, fo-o='arg')
```

#### Second error

The second error seems to come from the fact that `argparse.add_argument` treats `dest` [differently][2] depending on whether the argument is a positional argument or an optional one, but `Interface.base.setup_parser` doesn't account for this.

Fixing this error would make it easy to work around the first error by specifying `dest`.  If I'm thinking about this correctly, it should be enough for `setup_parser` to check whether the argument is a positional one and, if so, move `dest` from `parser_kwargs` to the first argument in `parser_args`.

    11	`flynt` is a command line tool to automatically convert a project's Python code from old "%-formatted" and .format(...) strings into Python 3.6+'s "f-strings".
    12	
    13	F-Strings:
    14	
    15	> Not only are they more readable, more concise, and less prone to error than other ways of formatting, but they are also faster!
    16	
    17	### Installation
    18	
    19	`pip install flynt`. It requires Python version 3.7+.
    20	
    21	### Usage
    22	
    23	*Flynt will modify the files it runs on. Add your project to version control system before using flynt.*
    24	
    25	To run: `flynt {source_file_or_directory}`
    26	
    27	* Given a single file, it will 'f-stringify' it: replace all applicable string formatting in this file (file will be modified).
    28	* Given a folder, it will search the folder recursively and f-stringify all the .py files it finds. It skips some hard-coded folder names: `blacklist = {'.tox', 'venv', 'site-packages', '.eggs'}`.
    29	
    30	It turns the code it runs on into Python 3.6+, since 3.6 is when "f-strings" were introduced.
    31	
    32	### Command line options
    33	
    34	From the output of `flynt -h`:
    35	
    36	<!-- begin-options -->
    37	```

    39	             [-s] [--no-tp] [--no-tf] [-tc] [-tj] [-f] [-a]
    40	             [-e EXCLUDE [EXCLUDE ...]] [--version]
    41	             [src ...]

    47	                        to read stdin and output to stdout)

    50	  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
    51	  -v, --verbose         run with verbose output
    52	  -q, --quiet           run without stdout output
    53	  --no-multiline        convert only single line expressions
    54	  -ll LINE_LENGTH, --line-length LINE_LENGTH
    55	                        for expressions spanning multiple lines,
    56	                        convert only if the resulting single line
    57	                        will fit into the line length limit. Default
    58	                        value is 88 characters.
    59	  -d, --dry-run         Do not change the files in-place and print

   125	### Pre-commit hook
   126	
   127	To make sure all formatted strings are always converted to f-strings, you can
   128	add flynt to your [pre-commit](https://www.pre-commit.com) hooks.
   129	
   130	Add a new section to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:
   131	```
   132	-   repo: https://github.com/ikamensh/flynt/
   133	    rev: ''
   134	    hooks:
   135	    -   id: flynt
   136	```
   137	
   138	This will run flynt on all modified files before committing.
   139	
   140	You can skip conversion of certain lines by adding `# noqa [: anything else] flynt [anything else]`
   141	
   142	
   143	### Configuration files
   144	
   145	Since v0.71 flynt can be configured using `pyproject.toml` file on a per-project basis. 
   146	Use same arguments as in CLI, and add them to `[tool.flynt]` section. CLI arguments takes precedence over the config file.
   147	It can also be configured globally with a toml file located in `~/.config/flynt.toml` on Unix / `~/.flynt.toml` on Windows.
   148	
   149	### About
   150	
   151	Read up on f-strings here:
   152	- https://realpython.com/python-f-strings/
   153	- https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0498/
   154	
   155	After obsessively refactoring a project at work, and not even covering 50% of f-string candidates, I realized there was some place for automation. Also it was very interesting to work with ast module.
   156	
   157	### Dangers of conversion
   158	It is not guaranteed that formatted strings will be exactly the same as before conversion.
   159	
   160	`'%s' % var` is converted to `f'{var}'`. There is a case when this will behave different from the original -  if var is a tuple of one element. In this case, %s displays the element, and f-string displays the tuple. Example:
   161	
   162	```
   163	foo = (1,)
   164	print('%s' % foo) # prints '1'
   165	print(f'{foo}')   # prints '(1,)'
   166	```
   167	
   168	Furthermore, some arguments cause formatting of strings to throw exceptions. One example where f-strings are inconsistent with previous formatting is %d vs {:d} - new format no longer accepts floats. While most cases are covered by taking the formatting specifiers to the f-strings format, the precise exception behaviour might differ as well. Make sure you have sufficient test coverage.

    20	The consensus was that a close collaboration that benefits the entire community can only be maximized through joint projects. The data import should include as many available data formats as possible, but the data export should be limited to the recognized standards, such as [ODIM_H5](https://www.eumetnet.eu/activities/observations-programme/current-activities/opera/) and [CfRadial](https://github.com/NCAR/CfRadial).

    13	### Components
    14	
    15	The fundamental building blocks of Zookeeper are components. The

    17	components. These component classes can have configurable parameters, which are
    18	declared using class-level type annotations (in a similar way to [Python
    19	dataclasses](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html)). These
    20	parameters can be Python objects or nested sub-components, and need not be set

    28	class ChildComponent:
    29	    a: int                  # An `int` parameter, with no default set
    30	    b: str = "foo"          # A `str` parameter, which by default will be `foo`
    31	
    32	@component
    33	class ParentComponent:
    34	    a: int                  # The same `int` parameter as the child
    35	    child: ChildComponent   # A nested component parameter, of type `ChildComponent`
    36	```
    37	
    38	After instantiation, components can be 'configured' with a configuration
    39	dictionary, containing values for a tree of nested parameters. This process
    40	automatically injects the correct values into each parameter.
    41	
    42	If a child sub-component declares a parameter which already exists in some
    43	containing parent, then it will pick up the value that's set on the parent,

    10	
    11	FreezeGun is a library that allows your Python tests to travel through time by mocking the datetime module.
    12	
    13	Usage
    14	-----
    15	
    16	Once the decorator or context manager have been invoked, all calls to datetime.datetime.now(), datetime.datetime.utcnow(), datetime.date.today(), time.time(), time.localtime(), time.gmtime(), and time.strftime() will return the time that has been frozen.
    17	
    18	Decorator
    19	~~~~~~~~~
    20	
    21	.. code-block:: python
    22	
    23	    from freezegun import freeze_time
    24	    import datetime
    25	    import unittest
    26	
    27	
    28	    @freeze_time("2012-01-14")
    29	    def test():
    30	        assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
    31	
    32	    # Or a unittest TestCase - freezes for every test, from the start of setUpClass to the end of tearDownClass
    33	
    34	    @freeze_time("1955-11-12")
    35	    class MyTests(unittest.TestCase):
    36	        def test_the_class(self):
    37	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(1955, 11, 12)
    38	
    39	    # Or any other class - freezes around each callable (may not work in every case)
    40	
    41	    @freeze_time("2012-01-14")
    42	    class Tester(object):
    43	        def test_the_class(self):
    44	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
    45	
    46	Context manager
    47	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    48	
    49	.. code-block:: python
    50	
    51	    from freezegun import freeze_time
    52	
    53	    def test():
    54	        assert datetime.datetime.now() != datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
    55	        with freeze_time("2012-01-14"):
    56	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
    57	        assert datetime.datetime.now() != datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
    58	
    59	Raw use
    60	~~~~~~~
    61	
    62	.. code-block:: python
    63	
    64	    from freezegun import freeze_time
    65	
    66	    freezer = freeze_time("2012-01-14 12:00:01")
    67	    freezer.start()
    68	    assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14, 12, 0, 1)
    69	    freezer.stop()
    70	
    71	Timezones
    72	~~~~~~~~~
    73

    97	    @freeze_time("Jan 14th, 2012")

   101	Function and generator objects
   102	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   103	
   104	FreezeGun is able to handle function and generator objects.
   105	
   106	.. code-block:: python
   107	
   108	    def test_lambda():
   109	        with freeze_time(lambda: datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)):
   110	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2012, 1, 14)
   111	
   112	    def test_generator():
   113	        datetimes = (datetime.datetime(year, 1, 1) for year in range(2010, 2012))
   114	
   115	        with freeze_time(datetimes):
   116	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2010, 1, 1)
   117	
   118	        with freeze_time(datetimes):
   119	            assert datetime.datetime.now() == datetime.datetime(2011, 1, 1)
   120	
   121	        # The next call to freeze_time(datetimes) would raise a StopIteration exception.
   122	
   123	``tick`` argument
   124	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   125	
   126	FreezeGun has an additional ``tick`` argument which will restart time at the given
   127	value, but then time will keep ticking. This is alternative to the default
   128	parameters which will keep time stopped.
   129	
   130	.. code-block:: python
   131	
   132	    @freeze_time("Jan 14th, 2020", tick=True)
   133	    def test_nice_datetime():
   134	        assert datetime.datetime.now() > datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 14)
   135	
   136	``auto_tick_seconds`` argument
   137	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   138	
   139	FreezeGun has an additional ``auto_tick_seconds`` argument which will autoincrement the
   140	value every time by the given amount from the start value. This is alternative to the default
   141	parameters which will keep time stopped. Note that given ``auto_tick_seconds`` the ``tick`` parameter will be ignored.
   142	
   143	.. code-block:: python
   144	
   145	    @freeze_time("Jan 14th, 2020", auto_tick_seconds=15)
   146	    def test_nice_datetime():
   147	        first_time = datetime.datetime.now()
   148	        auto_incremented_time = datetime.datetime.now()
   149	        assert first_time + datetime.timedelta(seconds=15) == auto_incremented_time
   150	
   151	
   152	Manual ticks
   153	~~~~~~~~~~~~
   154	
   155	FreezeGun allows for the time to be manually forwarded as well.
   156	
   157	.. code-block:: python
   158	
   159	    def test_manual_increment():
   160	        initial_datetime = datetime.datetime(year=1, month=7, day=12,
   161	                                            hour=15, minute=6, second=3)
   162	        with freeze_time(initial_datetime) as frozen_datetime:
   163	            assert frozen_datetime() == initial_datetime
   164	
   165	            frozen_datetime.tick()
   166	            initial_datetime += datetime.timedelta(seconds=1)
   167	            assert frozen_datetime() == initial_datetime
   168	
   169	            frozen_datetime.tick(delta=datetime.timedelta(seconds=10))
   170	            initial_datetime += datetime.timedelta(seconds=10)
   171	            assert frozen_datetime() == initial_datetime
   172	
   173	Moving time to specify datetime
   174	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   175	
   176	FreezeGun allows moving time to specific dates.
   177

   179

   182	                                            hour=15, minute=6, second=3)

   187	            assert frozen_datetime() == initial_datetime

   190	            assert frozen_datetime() == other_datetime
   191	
   192	            frozen_datetime.move_to(initial_datetime)
   193	            assert frozen_datetime() == initial_datetime

    45	### Tricks and Gotchas
    46	
    47	* Assigning to the same property repeatedly does NOT overwrite the value, instead it appends. To overwrite a value, instead set it to a false value first.
    48	
    49	
    50	### Factory settings
    51	
    52	There are quite a few settings for how the module works, which are managed by a `factory` object.  
    53	
    54	URI and File System Configuration:
    55	* `base_url` The base url on to which to append any slug given when an object is created
    56	* `base_dir` The base directory into which to write files, via factory.toFile()
    57	* `filename_extension` The extension to use on files written via toFile(), defaults to ".json"
    58	* `default_lang` The code for the default language to use on text values
    59	* `context_uri` The URI to use for `@context` in the JSON-LD serialization
    60	* `context_json` The parsed JSON object of the context from which the prefixes are derived
    61	* `full_names` Should the serialization use the full CRM names for classes and properties instead of the more readable ones defined in the mapping, defaults to False
    62	* `prefixes` A dictionary of prefix to URI for URIs to compress down to `prefix:slug` format
    63	* `prefixes_rev` The reverse of the prefixes dictionary
    64	* `pipe_scoped_contexts` A convenience setting for generating documentation, where properties that map to the same JSON output are represented as `short_name|full_name` to be post-processed.
    65	* `json_indent` How many spaces should each level of indentation be when serializing to a human readable form, defaults to 2
    66	* `id_type_label` Should the id, type and label properties all be used when serializing resources that have already been processed, defaults to True
    67	* `elasticsearch_compatible` Despite JSON-LD 1.0 compaction rules, should a single URI be represented as {"@id": "URI"} rather than just "URI", to make the resulting JSON compatible with elasticsearch and similar JSON processing engines. Defaults to False.
    68	* `serialize_all_resources` NOT YET IMPLEMENTED. If true, then all resources will be serialized separately, not just the top level resource.
    69	
    70	Model Validation and Generation:
    71	* `materialize_inverses` Should the inverse relationships be set automatically, defaults to False
    72	* `validate_properties` Should the model be validated at run time when setting properties, defaults to True  (this allows you to save processing time once you're certain your code does the right thing)
    73	* `validate_properties` Should the properties be validated as being part of the model at all
    74	* `validate_profile` Should the profile of which terms should be used be validated
    75	* `process_multiplicity` Should properties that allow multiple values always be an array
    76	* `validate_range` Should the object be validated that it is legal to be the value of the property
    77	* `auto_assign_id` Should a URI be autogenerated and assigned, defaults to True
    78	* `auto_id_type` The method by which the URI is generated, taken from the following values:
    79	  * "int" (just increment an integer in a single value space)
    80	  * "int-per-type" (increment an integer, with a separate value space per class)
    81	  * "int-per-segment" (increment an integer, with a separate value space per URI segment associated with a class)
    82	  * "uuid" (just use UUIDs everywhere)
    83	
    84	Internal:
    85	* `debug_level` Settings for debugging errors and warnings, defaults to "warn"
    86	* `log_stream` An object implementing the stream API to write log messages to, defaults to sys.stderr

    88	
    89	
    90	## How it Works
    91	
    92	At import time, the library parses the vocabulary data file (data/crm_vocab.tsv) and creates Python classes in the module's global scope from each of the defined RDF classes.  The names of the classes are intended to be easy to use and remember, not necessarily identical to the CRM ontology's names. It also records the properties that can be used with that class, and at run time checks whether the property is defined and that the value fits the defined range.

    95	
    96	You can change the mapping by tweaking `utils/vocab_reader.py` and rerunning it to build a new TSV input file.  See also the experimental code for loading completely different ontologies.

If you don't have `flake8` already, it will install automatically when you install `pandas-vet`. 30 31 The plugin is on PyPI and can be installed with: 32 33 ```bash 34 pip install pandas-vet 35 ``` 36 37 It can also be installed with `conda`: 38 39 ```bash 40 conda install -c conda-forge pandas-vet 41 ``` 42 43 `pandas-vet` is tested under Python 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, and 3.11 as defined in our [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/deppen8/pandas-vet/blob/main/.github/workflows/testing.yml) 44 45 ## Usage 46 47 Once installed successfully in an environment that also has `flake8` installed, `pandas-vet` should run whenever `flake8` is run. 48 49 ```bash 50 flake8 ... 51 ``` 52 53 See the [`flake8` docs](http://flake8.pycqa.org/en/latest/user/invocation.html) for more information. 54 55 For a full list of implemented warnings, see [the list below](#list-of-warnings). 56 57 ## Contributing 58 59 `pandas-vet` is still in the very early stages. **Problem Statement:**
The issue is that when a Swagger/OpenAPI specification is provided in YAML format with **integer** response status codes (e.g., `200`, `404`), the JSON schema validator crashes because it expects all keys in the swagger specification to be **strings**.

**Key Technical Details:**
- **Component**: JSON schema validator in oasapi
- **Trigger**: YAML files with integer status codes (e.g., `200:` instead of `"200":`)
- **Expected behavior**: Status codes should be treated as strings in the JSON schema
- **Actual behavior**: Exception/crash occurs during validation

**Root Cause:**
In YAML, unquoted numeric values are parsed as integers. When a YAML file has:
```yaml
responses:
  200:
    description: Success
```
YAML parses `200` as an integer, but JSON schema validators expect dictionary keys to be strings.

**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. Create a YAML Swagger spec with integer status codes (no quotes around status codes)
2. Load the YAML file
3. Pass it to the oasapi validator
4. Observe the exception

**Best Practices for Fix:**
- Convert integer keys to strings before validation
- Handle this conversion at the appropriate layer (likely during YAML loading or before validation)
- Ensure backward compatibility with existing string status codes
- Minimal changes to preserve existing functionality

   128	* the table has no primary key constraint (which is required by SQLAlchemy for every
   129	  model class)
   130	* the table is an association table between two other tables (see below for the
   131	  specifics)
   132	
   133	Model class naming logic
   134	++++++++++++++++++++++++
   135	
   136	By default, table names are converted to valid PEP 8 compliant class names by replacing
   137	all characters unsuitable for Python identifiers with ``_``. Then, each valid parts
   138	(separated by underscores) are title cased and then joined together, eliminating the
   139	underscores. So, ``example_name`` becomes ``ExampleName``.
   140	
   141	If the ``use_inflect`` option is used, the table name (which is assumed to be in
   142	English) is converted to singular form using the "inflect" library. For example,
   143	``sales_invoices`` becomes ``SalesInvoice``. Since table names are not always in
   144	English, and the inflection process is far from perfect, inflection is disabled by
   145	default.
   146	
   147	Relationship detection logic
   148	++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
   149	
   150	Relationships are detected based on existing foreign key constraints as follows:
   151	
   152	* **many-to-one**: a foreign key constraint exists on the table
   153	* **one-to-one**: same as **many-to-one**, but a unique constraint exists on the
   154	  column(s) involved
   155	* **many-to-many**: (not implemented on the ``sqlmodel`` generator) an association table
   156	  is found to exist between two tables

   158	A table is considered an association table if it satisfies all of the following
   159	conditions:
   160	
   161	#. has exactly two foreign key constraints
   162	#. all its columns are involved in said constraints
   163	
   164	Relationship naming logic
   165	+++++++++++++++++++++++++
   166	
   167	Relationships are typically named based on the table name of the opposite class.
   168	For example, if a class has a relationship to another class with the table named
   169	``companies``, the relationship would be named ``companies`` (unless the ``use_inflect``
   170	option was enabled, in which case it would be named ``company`` in the case of a
   171	many-to-one or one-to-one relationship).

   174	if the column is named like ``employer_id``. Then the relationship is named ``employer``
   175	due to that ``_id`` suffix.
   176

   178	with the ``_reverse`` suffix appended to it.

<issue_description>
Feature flag framework
To check for the availability of a feature in UI, we do this:

```jinja2
{% if obj.view_for('action').is_available() %}
```

These work when the block contains a link to the feature page, but sometimes the entire feature is contained in the template, and the tests get too complex. Sample from Funnel:

```jinja2
{%- if (project.boxoffice_data and project.boxoffice_data.item_collection_id) or project.schedule_state.PUBLISHED -%}
```

As these tend to repeat throughout the template, they should be defined in a central place. The model is a tempting choice as the instance is available and we already have a framework like state manager, but this is a view concern and should be defined in views.

## Option A: Re-use ModelView and RegistryMixin

ModelView registration is already supported via [RegistryMixin](https://github.com/hasgeek/coaster/blob/5952d8eb7ed51b8405ace6d82ab71843abe971e2/coaster/sqlalchemy/registry.py). It can be used to add feature detection methods:

```python
class MyModelView(ModelView):
    model = Model
    def has_feature(self):
        if self.view_name.is_available():
            return True
        # Or...
        if self.obj.state.PUBLISHED and (other_extended_criteria):
            return True

Model.views.main = ModelView
```
```jinja2
{% if obj.views.main.has_feature() %}
```

## Option B: Add a new registry

The existing `forms` and `views` registries can be complemented with a `features` registry. Registering functions on it will reduce the expense of class instantiation:

```python
Model.features.has_feature_name = lambda obj: obj.state.PUBLISHED
```

The Registry class can be amended to serve as a decorator, making it easier to add complex feature tests. Note that Registry passes an explicit `obj` parameter, so the test function must accept `obj`:

```python
@Model.features()
def has_feature_name(obj):
    …

@Model.features('other_feature')
def other_feature_test(obj):
    …
```

The decorator will use the function's name if no explicit name is provided. Adding a decorator will also make view registration straightforward.

```python
@Model.views('main')
@route('/<model>')
class MyModelView(ModelView):
    model = Model
    …
```

An advanced use case is feature versioning, to perform A/B tests. This can be simplistically achieved with:

```jinja2
{% if obj.features.has_feature() %}
  {% if obj.features.has_feature_v1() %}
    …
  {% endif %}
  {% if obj.features.has_feature_v2() %}
    …
  {% endif %}
{% endif %}
```

Where `my_feature()` tests for feature availability, and the distinct `_v1` and `_v2` functions test for the bucket the user has been assigned to. To avoid overhead, they can skip testing for feature availability itself, leaving that to the parent test.

Note: while the feature test functions are lighter than class instantiation, they may still need the class view when testing for roles:

```python
@Model.features()
def can_edit(obj):
    return MyModelView(obj).edit.is_available()
```
</issue_description>

     7	---------
     8	
     9	py_zipkin provides a context manager/decorator along with some utilities to
    10	facilitate the usage of Zipkin in Python applications.
    11	
    12	Install
    13	-------
    14	
    15	```
    16	pip install py_zipkin
    17	```
    18	
    19	Usage
    20	-----
    21	
    22	py_zipkin requires a `transport_handler` object that handles logging zipkin
    23	messages to a central logging service such as kafka or scribe.
    24	
    25	`py_zipkin.zipkin.zipkin_span` is the main tool for starting zipkin traces or
    26	logging spans inside an ongoing trace. zipkin_span can be used as a context
    27	manager or a decorator.
    28	
    29	#### Usage #1: Start a trace with a given sampling rate
    30	
    31	```python
    32	from py_zipkin.zipkin import zipkin_span
    33	
    34	def some_function(a, b):
    35	    with zipkin_span(
    36	        service_name='my_service',
    37	        span_name='my_span_name',
    38	        transport_handler=some_handler,
    39	        port=42,
    40	        sample_rate=0.05, # Value between 0.0 and 100.0
    41	    ):
    42	        do_stuff(a, b)
    43	```
    44	
    45	#### Usage #2: Trace a service call
    46	
    47	The difference between this and Usage #1 is that the zipkin_attrs are calculated
    48	separately and passed in, thus negating the need of the sample_rate param.
    49	
    50	```python
    51	# Define a pyramid tween
    52	def tween(request):
    53	    zipkin_attrs = some_zipkin_attr_creator(request)
    54	    with zipkin_span(
    55	        service_name='my_service',
    56	        span_name='my_span_name',
    57	        zipkin_attrs=zipkin_attrs,
    58	        transport_handler=some_handler,
    59	        port=22,
    60	    ) as zipkin_context:
    61	        response = handler(request)
    62	        zipkin_context.update_binary_annotations(
    63	            some_binary_annotations)
    64	        return response
    65	```
    66	
    67	#### Usage #3: Log a span inside an ongoing trace
    68	
    69	This can be also be used inside itself to produce continuously nested spans.
    70	
    71	```python
    72	@zipkin_span(service_name='my_service', span_name='some_function')
    73	def some_function(a, b):
    74	    return do_stuff(a, b)
    75	```

    78

    83	def some_function(a, b):
    84	    with zipkin_span(

    87	        transport_handler=some_handler,

   134	Transport
   135	---------
   136	
   137	py_zipkin (for the moment) thrift-encodes spans. The actual transport layer is
   138	pluggable, though.
   139	
   140	The recommended way to implement a new transport handler is to subclass
   141	`py_zipkin.transport.BaseTransportHandler` and implement the `send` and 
   142	`get_max_payload_bytes` methods.
   143	
   144	`send` receives an already encoded thrift list as argument.
   145	`get_max_payload_bytes` should return the maximum payload size supported by your
   146	transport, or `None` if you can send arbitrarily big messages.
   147	
   148	The simplest way to get spans to the collector is via HTTP POST. Here's an
   149	example of a simple HTTP transport using the `requests` library. This assumes
   150	your Zipkin collector is running at localhost:9411.
   151	
   152	> NOTE: older versions of py_zipkin suggested implementing the transport handler
   153	> as a function with a single argument. That's still supported and should work
   154	> with the current py_zipkin version, but it's deprecated. 
   155	
   156	```python
   157	import requests
   158	
   159	from py_zipkin.transport import BaseTransportHandler
   160	
   161	
   162	class HttpTransport(BaseTransportHandler):
   163	
   164	    def get_max_payload_bytes(self):
   165	        return None
   166	
   167	    def send(self, encoded_span):
   168	        # The collector expects a thrift-encoded list of spans.
   169	        requests.post(
   170	            'http://localhost:9411/api/v1/spans',
   171	            data=encoded_span,
   172	            headers={'Content-Type': 'application/x-thrift'},
   173	        )
   174	```

   177	in production), you'd do something like the following, using the
   178	[kafka-python](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/kafka-python) package:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	from kafka import SimpleProducer, KafkaClient
   182	
   183	from py_zipkin.transport import BaseTransportHandler
   184	
   185	
   186	class KafkaTransport(BaseTransportHandler):
   187	
   188	    def get_max_payload_bytes(self):
   189	        # By default Kafka rejects messages bigger than 1000012 bytes.
   190	        return 1000012
   191	
   192	    def send(self, message):
   193	        kafka_client = KafkaClient('{}:{}'.format('localhost', 9092))
   194	        producer = SimpleProducer(kafka_client)
   195	        producer.send_messages('kafka_topic_name', message)
   196	```

   198	Using in multithreading evironments
   199	-----------------------------------
   200	
   201	If you want to use py_zipkin in a cooperative multithreading environment,
   202	e.g. asyncio, you need to explicitly pass an instance of `py_zipkin.storage.Stack`
   203	as parameter `context_stack` for `zipkin_span` and `create_http_headers_for_new_span`.
   204	By default, py_zipkin uses a thread local storage for the attributes, which is
   205	defined in `py_zipkin.storage.ThreadLocalStack`.

   207	Additionally, you'll also need to explicitly pass an instance of
   208	`py_zipkin.storage.SpanStorage` as parameter `span_storage` to `zipkin_span`.
   209	
   210	```python
   211	from py_zipkin.zipkin import zipkin_span
   212	from py_zipkin.storage import Stack
   213	from py_zipkin.storage import SpanStorage
   214	
   215	
   216	def my_function():
   217	    context_stack = Stack()
   218	    span_storage = SpanStorage()
   219	    await my_function(context_stack, span_storage)

   223	        service_name='my_service',
   224	        span_name='some_function',
   225	        transport_handler=some_handler,
   226	        port=42,
   227	        sample_rate=0.05,
   228	        context_stack=context_stack,
   229	        span_storage=span_storage,

   238	"Firehose mode" records 100% of the spans, regardless of

In https://github.com/dask/dask-ml/blob/master/dask_ml/model_selection/_normalize.py#L18-L24, we register a tokenizer for scikit-learn models that inherit from BaseEstimator. This can cause issues when we have multiple instances of the same model that have been fitted to different pieces of data (as in https://github.com/dask/dask-ml/pull/657).

```python

   ...:
   ...: # Not fitted, fine for these to match
   ...: assert dask.base.tokenize(m1) == dask.base.tokenize(m2)
   ...:
   ...: X1, y1 = sklearn.datasets.make_classification()
   ...: X2, y2 = sklearn.datasets.make_classification()
   ...: m1.fit(X1, y1)
   ...: m2.fit(X2, y2)

I think that `normalize_estimator` should also (try to) hash things like `coef_`. ```python

  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.7/site-packages/papermill/cli.py", line 228, in papermill
    parameters_final.update(read_yaml_file(files))
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable
```

The reason for this is that papermill [uses the result of `yaml.load` to update the `parameters_final` dictionary](https://github.com/nteract/papermill/blob/main/papermill/cli.py#L227). When the input to `yaml.load` is empty (either the file is empty or just has some boilerplate comments but no named parameters), then `yaml.load` returns `None`, i.e.

```python
import yaml

# These both evaluate to None
yaml.load('', Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)
yaml.load('# There are no configurable parameters for this notebook', Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)
```

This is a minor gripe and I can work around it, but it would make my orchestration code a lot easier to read if I could just do this and not have to worry about empty files:

```bash
for action in train evaluate do_something_else; do
    papermill "input/${action}.ipynb" "output/${action}.ipynb" --parameters_file "config/${action}.yml"
done
```

The fix here seems easy enough - just change any call to `yaml.load(...)` to `yaml.load(...) or {}`, i.e.

```python
...
parameters_final.update(yaml.load(base64.b64decode(params), Loader=NoDatesSafeLoader) or {})
...
parameters_final.update(read_yaml_file(files) or {})
...
parameters_final.update(yaml.load(params, Loader=NoDatesSafeLoader) or {})
...
```

    16	**papermill** is a tool for parameterizing, executing, and analyzing
    17	Jupyter Notebooks.
    18	
    19	Papermill lets you:
    20	
    21	-   **parameterize** notebooks
    22	-   **execute** notebooks
    23	
    24	This opens up new opportunities for how notebooks can be used. For
    25	example:
    26	
    27	-   Perhaps you have a financial report that you wish to run with
    28	    different values on the first or last day of a month or at the
    29	    beginning or end of the year, **using parameters** makes this task
    30	    easier.
    31	-   Do you want to run a notebook and depending on its results, choose a
    32	    particular notebook to run next? You can now programmatically
    33	    **execute a workflow** without having to copy and paste from
    34	    notebook to notebook manually.
    35	
    36	Papermill takes an *opinionated* approach to notebook parameterization and
    37	execution based on our experiences using notebooks at scale in data
    38	pipelines.
    39	
    40	## Installation
    41	
    42	From the command line:
    43	
    44	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
    45	pip install papermill
    46	```
    47	
    48	For all optional io dependencies, you can specify individual bundles
    49	like `s3`, or `azure` -- or use `all`
    50	
    51	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
    52	pip install papermill[all]
    53	```
    54	
    55	## Python Version Support
    56	
    57	This library currently supports Python 3.5+ versions. As minor Python
    58	versions are officially sunset by the Python org papermill will similarly
    59	drop support in the future.
    60	
    61	## Usage
    62	
    63	### Parameterizing a Notebook
    64	
    65	To parameterize your notebook designate a cell with the tag ``parameters``.
    66	
    67	![enable parameters in Jupyter](docs/img/enable_parameters.gif)
    68	
    69	Papermill looks for the ``parameters`` cell and treats this cell as defaults for the parameters passed in at execution time. Papermill will add a new cell tagged with ``injected-parameters`` with input parameters in order to overwrite the values in ``parameters``. If no cell is tagged with ``parameters`` the injected cell will be inserted at the top of the notebook.
    70	
    71	Additionally, if you rerun notebooks through papermill and it will reuse the ``injected-parameters`` cell from the prior run. In this case Papermill will replace the old ``injected-parameters`` cell with the new run's inputs.
    72	
    73	![image](docs/img/parameters.png)
    74	
    75	### Executing a Notebook
    76	
    77	The two ways to execute the notebook with parameters are: (1) through
    78	the Python API and (2) through the command line interface.
    79	
    80	#### Execute via the Python API
    81	
    82	``` {.sourceCode .python}
    83	import papermill as pm
    84	
    85	pm.execute_notebook(
    86	   'path/to/input.ipynb',
    87	   'path/to/output.ipynb',
    88	   parameters = dict(alpha=0.6, ratio=0.1)
    89	)
    90	```
    91	
    92	#### Execute via CLI
    93	
    94	Here's an example of a local notebook being executed and output to an
    95	Amazon S3 account:
    96	
    97	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
    98	$ papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -p alpha 0.6 -p l1_ratio 0.1
    99	```
   100	
   101	**NOTE:**
   102	If you use multiple AWS accounts, and you have [properly configured your AWS  credentials](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/guide/configuration.html), then you can specify which account to use by setting the `AWS_PROFILE` environment variable at the command-line. For example:
   103	
   104	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
   105	$ AWS_PROFILE=dev_account papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -p alpha 0.6 -p l1_ratio 0.1
   106	```
   107	
   108	In the above example, two parameters are set: ``alpha`` and ``l1_ratio`` using ``-p`` (``--parameters`` also works). Parameter values that look like booleans or numbers will be interpreted as such. Here are the different ways users may set parameters:
   109	
   110	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
   111	$ papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -r version 1.0
   112	```
   113	
   114	Using ``-r`` or ``--parameters_raw``, users can set parameters one by one. However, unlike ``-p``, the parameter will remain a string, even if it may be interpreted as a number or boolean.
   115	
   116	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
   117	$ papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -f parameters.yaml
   118	```
   119	
   120	Using ``-f`` or ``--parameters_file``, users can provide a YAML file from which parameter values should be read.
   121	
   122	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
   123	$ papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -y "
   124	alpha: 0.6
   125	l1_ratio: 0.1"
   126	```
   127	
   128	Using ``-y`` or ``--parameters_yaml``, users can directly provide a YAML string containing parameter values.
   129	
   130	``` {.sourceCode .bash}
   131	$ papermill local/input.ipynb s3://bkt/output.ipynb -b YWxwaGE6IDAuNgpsMV9yYXRpbzogMC4xCg==
   132	```
   133	
   134	Using ``-b`` or ``--parameters_base64``, users can provide a YAML string, base64-encoded, containing parameter values.
   135	
   136	When using YAML to pass arguments, through ``-y``, ``-b`` or ``-f``, parameter values can be arrays or dictionaries:

   145	linear_function:

The issue describes a **thread safety problem** with `app.current_request` in Chalice:

- **Core Problem**: When running Chalice locally and handling multiple concurrent requests, `app.current_request` is a shared global variable that can be overwritten by subsequent requests before earlier requests finish processing
- **Example Scenario**: 
  1. Request 1 arrives and starts being handled
  2. Request 2 arrives and overwrites `app.current_request`
  3. Request 3 arrives and overwrites `app.current_request` again
  4. Handler for Request 2 reads `app.current_request` but gets Request 3's context instead
- **Key Technical Details**:
  - Variable: `app.current_request`
  - Context: Running with `chalice local` (local development server)
  - Problem: Race condition in concurrent request handling
  - Question: Whether this is also an issue in Lambda (likely not, since Lambda typically uses separate processes)

**1.3: Clear Problem Statement**
The `app.current_request` attribute is a global/shared state that gets overwritten when multiple requests are handled concurrently, causing handlers to access the wrong request context.

**1.4: Steps to Reproduce**
1. Start a Chalice app locally
2. Send multiple concurrent requests
3. In a handler, access `app.current_request` after some async/delayed operation
4. Observe that `app.current_request` may contain data from a different request

**1.5: Best Practices**
- Use thread-local storage for request-specific data
- Consider passing request objects as parameters instead of using global state
- Ensure backward compatibility with existing code

     1	# genanki: A Library for Generating Anki Decks
     2	
     3	`genanki` allows you to programatically generate decks in Python 3 for Anki, a popular spaced-repetition flashcard
     4	program. Please see below for concepts and usage.
     5	
     6	*This library and its author(s) are not affiliated/associated with the main Anki project in any way.*
     7	
     8	[![CI](https://github.com/kerrickstaley/genanki/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/kerrickstaley/genanki/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
     9	
    10	## Notes
    11	The basic unit in Anki is the `Note`, which contains a fact to memorize. `Note`s correspond to one or more `Card`s.
    12	
    13	Here's how you create a `Note`:
    14	
    15	```python
    16	my_note = genanki.Note(
    17	  model=my_model,
    18	  fields=['Capital of Argentina', 'Buenos Aires'])
    19	```
    20	
    21	You pass in a `Model`, discussed below, and a set of `fields` (encoded as HTML).
    22	
    23	## Models
    24	A `Model` defines the fields and cards for a type of `Note`. For example:
    25	
    26	```python
    27	my_model = genanki.Model(
    28	  1607392319,
    29	  'Simple Model',
    30	  fields=[
    31	    {'name': 'Question'},
    32	    {'name': 'Answer'},
    33	  ],
    34	  templates=[
    35	    {
    36	      'name': 'Card 1',
    37	      'qfmt': '{{Question}}',
    38	      'afmt': '{{FrontSide}}<hr id="answer">{{Answer}}',
    39	    },
    40	  ])
    41	```
    42	
    43	This note-type has two fields and one card. The card displays the `Question` field on the front and the `Question` and
    44	`Answer` fields on the back, separated by a `<hr>`. You can also pass a `css` argument to `Model()` to supply custom
    45	CSS.
    46	
    47	You need to pass a `model_id` so that Anki can keep track of your model. It's important that you use a unique `model_id`
    48	for each `Model` you define. Use `import random; random.randrange(1 << 30, 1 << 31)` to generate a suitable model_id, and hardcode it
    49	into your `Model` definition.
    50	
    51	## Generating a Deck/Package
    52	To import your notes into Anki, you need to add them to a `Deck`:
    53	
    54	```python
    55	my_deck = genanki.Deck(
    56	  2059400110,
    57	  'Country Capitals')
    58	
    59	my_deck.add_note(my_note)
    60	```
    61	
    62	Once again, you need a unique `deck_id` that you should generate once and then hardcode into your `.py` file.
    63	
    64	Then, create a `Package` for your `Deck` and write it to a file:
    65	
    66	```python
    67	genanki.Package(my_deck).write_to_file('output.apkg')
    68	```
    69	
    70	You can then load `output.apkg` into Anki using File -> Import...
    71	
    72	## Media Files
    73	To add sounds or images, set the `media_files` attribute on your `Package`:
    74	
    75	```python
    76	my_package = genanki.Package(my_deck)
    77	my_package.media_files = ['sound.mp3', 'images/image.jpg']
    78	```
    79	
    80	`media_files` should have the path (relative or absolute) to each file. To use them in notes, first add a field to your model, and reference that field in your template:
    81	
    82	```python
    83	my_model = genanki.Model(
    84	  1091735104,
    85	  'Simple Model with Media',
    86	  fields=[
    87	    {'name': 'Question'},
    88	    {'name': 'Answer'},
    89	    {'name': 'MyMedia'},                                  # ADD THIS
    90	  ],
    91	  templates=[
    92	    {
    93	      'name': 'Card 1',
    94	      'qfmt': '{{Question}}<br>{{MyMedia}}',              # AND THIS
    95	      'afmt': '{{FrontSide}}<hr id="answer">{{Answer}}',
    96	    },
    97	  ])
    98	```
    99	
   100	Then, set the `MyMedia` field on your card to `[sound:sound.mp3]` for audio and `<img src="image.jpg">` for images.
   101	
   102	You *cannot* put `<img src="{MyMedia}">` in the template and `image.jpg` in the field. See these sections in the Anki manual for more information: [Importing Media](https://docs.ankiweb.net/#/importing?id=importing-media) and [Media & LaTeX](https://docs.ankiweb.net/#/templates/fields?id=media-amp-latex).
   103	
   104	You should only put the filename (aka basename) and not the full path in the field; `<img src="images/image.jpg">` will *not* work. Media files should have unique filenames.
   105	
   106	## Note GUIDs
   107	`Note`s have a `guid` property that uniquely identifies the note. If you import a new note that has the same GUID as an
   108	existing note, the new note will overwrite the old one (as long as their models have the same fields).
   109	
   110	This is an important feature if you want to be able to tweak the design/content of your notes, regenerate your deck, and
   111	import the updated version into Anki. Your notes need to have stable GUIDs in order for the new note to replace the
   112	existing one.
   113	
   114	By default, the GUID is a hash of all the field values. This may not be desirable if, for example, you add a new field
   115	with additional info that doesn't change the identity of the note. You can create a custom GUID implementation to hash
   116	only the fields that identify the note:
   117	
   118	```python
   119	class MyNote(genanki.Note):
   120	  @property
   121	  def guid(self):
   122	    return genanki.guid_for(self.fields[0], self.fields[1])
   123	```
   124	
   125	## sort_field
   126	Anki has a value for each `Note` called the `sort_field`. Anki uses this value to sort the cards in the Browse
   127	interface. Anki also is happier if you avoid having two notes with the same `sort_field`, although this isn't strictly
   128	necessary. By default, the `sort_field` is the first field, but you can change it by passing `sort_field=` to `Note()`
   129	or implementing `sort_field` as a property in a subclass (similar to `guid`).
   130	
   131	You can also pass `sort_field_index=` to `Model()` to change the sort field. `0` means the first field in the Note, `1` means the second, etc.
   132	
   133	## YAML for Templates (and Fields)
   134	You can create your template definitions in the YAML format and pass them as a `str` to `Model()`. You can also do this
   135	for fields.
   136	
   137	## Using genanki inside an Anki addon
   138	`genanki` supports adding generated notes to the local collection when running inside an Anki 2.1 addon (Anki 2.0
   139	may work but has not been tested). See the [`.write_to_collection_from_addon() method`](

   141	
   142	## FAQ
   143	### My field data is getting garbled
   144	If fields in your notes contain literal `<`, `>`, or `&` characters, you need to HTML-encode them: field data is HTML, not plain text. You can use the [`html.escape`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/html.html#html.escape) function.
   145	
   146	For example, you should write
   147	```
   148	fields=['AT&T was originally called', 'Bell Telephone Company']
   149	```
   150	or
   151	```
   152	fields=[html.escape(f) for f in ['AT&T was originally called', 'Bell Telephone Company']]
   153	```
   154	
   155	This applies even if the content is LaTeX; for example, you should write
   156	```
   157	fields=['Piketty calls this the "central contradiction of capitalism".', '[latex]r > g[/latex]']
   158	```

   164	python3 setup.py sdist bdist_wheel
