    92	## Validation
    93	
    94	### Basic checks
    95	
    96	The basic checks can't be disabled, as they deal with goodtables being able to read the files.
    97	
    98	| check | description |
    99	| --- | --- |
   100	| io-error | Data reading error because of IO error. |
   101	| http-error | Data reading error because of HTTP error. |
   102	| source-error | Data reading error because of not supported or inconsistent contents. |
   103	| scheme-error | Data reading error because of incorrect scheme. |
   104	| format-error | Data reading error because of incorrect format. |
   105	| encoding-error | Data reading error because of an encoding problem. |
   106	
   107	### Structural checks
   108	
   109	These checks validate that the structure of the file are valid.
   110	
   111	| check | description |
   112	| --- | --- |
   113	| blank-header | There is a blank header name. All cells in the header row must have a value. |
   114	| duplicate-header | There are multiple columns with the same name. All column names must be unique. |
   115	| blank-row | Rows must have at least one non-blank cell. |
   116	| duplicate-row | Rows can't be duplicated. |
   117	| extra-value | A row has more columns than the header. |
   118	| missing-value | A row has less columns than the header. |
   119	
   120	### Content checks
   121	
   122	These checks validate the contents of the file. To use them, you need to pass a [Table Schema][tableschema]. If you don't have a schema, goodtables can infer it if you use the `infer_schema` option.
   123	
   124	If your schema only covers part of the data, you can use the `infer_fields` to infer the remaining fields.
   125	
   126	Lastly, if the order of the fields in the data is different than in your schema, enable the `order_fields` option.
   127	
   128	| check | description |
   129	| --- | --- |
   130	| schema-error | Schema is not valid. |
   131	| non-matching-header | The header's name in the schema is different from what's in the data. |
   132	| extra-header | The data contains a header not defined in the schema. |
   133	| missing-header | The data doesn't contain a header defined in the schema. |
   134	| type-or-format-error | The value can’t be cast based on the schema type and format for this field. |
   135	| required-constraint | This field is a required field, but it contains no value. |
   136	| pattern-constraint | This field value's should conform to the defined pattern. |
   137	| unique-constraint | This field is a unique field but it contains a value that has been used in another row. |
   138	| enumerable-constraint | This field value should be equal to one of the values in the enumeration constraint. |
   139	| minimum-constraint | This field value should be greater or equal than constraint value. |
   140	| maximum-constraint | This field value should be less or equal than constraint value. |
   141	| minimum-length-constraint | A length of this field value should be greater or equal than schema constraint value. |
   142	| maximum-length-constraint | A length of this field value should be less or equal than schema constraint value. |
   143	
   144	### Advanced checks
   145	
   146	| check | description |
   147	| --- | --- |
   148	| [blacklisted-value](#blacklisted-value) | Ensure there are no cells with the blacklisted values. |
   149	| [deviated-value](#deviated-value) | Ensure numbers are within a number of standard deviations from the average. |
   150	| [foreign-key](#foreign-key) | Ensure foreign keys are valid within a data package |
   151	| [sequential-value](#sequential-value) | Ensure numbers are sequential. |
   152	| [truncated-value](#truncated-value) | Detect values that were potentially truncated. |
   153	| [custom-constraint](#custom-constraint) | Defines a constraint based on the values of other columns (e.g. `value * quantity == total`). |
   154	
   155	#### blacklisted-value
   156	
   157	Sometimes we have to check for some values we don't want to have in out dataset. It accepts following options:
   158	
   159	| option | type | description |
   160	| --- | --- | --- |
   161	| column | int/str | Column number or name |
   162	| blacklist | list of str | List of blacklisted values |
   163	
   164	Consider the following CSV file:
   165	
   166	```csv
   167	id,name
   168	1,John
   169	2,bug
   170	3,bad
   171	5,Alex
   172	```
   173	
   174	Let's check that the `name` column doesn't contain rows with `bug` or `bad`:
   175	
   176	```python
   177	from goodtables import validate
   178	
   179	report = validate('data.csv', checks=[
   180	    {'blacklisted-value': {'column': 'name', 'blacklist': ['bug', 'bad']}},
   181	])
   182	# error on row 3 with code "blacklisted-value"
   183	# error on row 4 with code "blacklisted-value"
   184	```
   185	
   186	#### deviated-value
   187	
   188	This check helps to find outlines in a column containing positive numbers. It accepts following options:
   189	
   190	| option | type | description |
   191	| --- | --- | --- |
   192	| column | int/str | Column number or name |
   193	| average | str | Average type, either "mean", "median" or "mode" |
   194	| interval | int | Values must be inside range `average ± standard deviation * interval` |
   195	
   196	Consider the following CSV file:
   197	
   198	```csv
   199	temperature
   200	1
   201	-2
   202	7
   203	0
   204	1
   205	2
   206	5
   207	-4
   208	100
   209	8
   210	3
   211	```
   212	
   213	We use `median` to get an average of the column values and allow interval of 3 standard deviations. For our case median is `2.0` and standard deviation is `29.73` so all valid values must be inside the `[-87.19, 91.19]` interval.
   214	
   215	```python
   216	report = validate('data.csv', checks=[
   217	    {'deviated-value': {'column': 'temperature', 'average': 'median', 'interval': 3}},
   218	])
   219	# error on row 10 with code "deviated-value"
   220	```

Some example below illustrate this: 

```python
import marshmallow
import marshmallow_dataclass

@marshmallow_dataclass.dataclass
class Person:
	name: str

	@marshmallow.post_load
	def a(schema, data, **kwargs):
		data.name = data.name.capitalize()  # works if: data['name'] = data['name'].capitalize()
		return data

Person.Schema().load({'name': 'matt'})
>> AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'name'
```

```python
import marshmallow
import marshmallow_dataclass

@marshmallow_dataclass.dataclass
class Person:
	name: str

	@marshmallow.post_load
	def z(schema, data, **kwargs):
		data.name = data.name.capitalize()
		return data

Person.Schema().load({'name': 'matt'})
>> Person(name='Matt')
```

The post_load in the first example does not create an instance of the dataclass itself before being invoked and feels more so like a `pre_load` because of this. The validation checks still seem to work properly, but it just feels a little weird to work with. I know the documentation does not include anything about pre/post loading, but I figured I'd document this in case anyone else runs into the same issue.

The issue describes a problem with the execution order of `post_load` decorators in marshmallow dataclass:

4. Rename the method to come later alphabetically (like `z`)  
5. Observe it works correctly with dataclass instances

- Ensure consistent execution order regardless of method names
- User post_load methods should always receive dataclass instances
- Maintain backward compatibility
- Test with various method names to ensure ordering independence

     3	
     4	Quantifiers are dependencies, injectable into prediction calls,
     5	which calculate predictions and uncertainties or confidences
     6	from DNN outputs:
     7	
     8	.. code-block:: python
     9	   :caption: Use of quantifiers on uwiz models
    10	
    11	    # Let's use a quantifier that calculates the entropy on a regression variable as uncertainty
    12	    predictions, entropy = model.predict_quantified(x_test, quantifier='predictive_entropy')
    13	
    14	    # Equivalently, we can pass the quantifier as object
    15	    quantifier = uwiz.quantifiers.PredictiveEntropy()
    16	    predictions, entropy = model.predict_quantified(x_test, quantifier=quantifer)
    17	
    18	    # We can also pass multiple quantifiers.
    19	    # In that case, `predict_quantified` returns a (prediction, confidence_or_uncertainty) tuple
    20	    # for every passed quantifier.
    21	    results = model.predict_quantified(x_test, quantifier=['predictive_entropy', 'mean_softmax')
    22	    # results[0] is a tuple of predictions and entropies
    23	    # results[1] is a tuple of predictions and mean softmax values
    24	
    25	Besides the prediction, quantifiers quantify either the networks confidence or its uncertainty.
    26	The difference between that two is as follows
    27	(assuming that the quantifier actually correctly captures the chance of misprediction):
    28	
    29	- In `uncertainty quantification`, the higher the value, the higher the chance of misprediction.
    30	- In `confidence quantification` the lower the value, the higher the chance of misprediction.
    31	
    32	For most applications where you use multiple quantifiers, you probably want to quantify
    33	either uncertainties or confidences to allow to use the quantifiers outputs interchangeable.
    34	Setting the param ``model.predict_quantified(..., as_confidence=True)``
    35	convert uncertainties into confidences. ``as_confidence=False`` converts confidences into uncertainties.
    36	The default is 'None', in which case no conversions are made.
    37	
    38	.. note::
    39	    Independent on how many quantifiers you pass to the `predict_quantified` method,
    40	    the outputs of the neural networks inference are re-used wherever possible for a more efficient execution.
    41	    Thus, it is better to call `predict_quantified` with two quantifiers than
    42	    to call `predict_quantified` twice, with one quantifier each.

   275	``premailer`` uses to parse CSS. It will use the python ``logging`` module
   276	to mention all issues it has with parsing your CSS. If you want to capture
   277	this, you have to pass in ``cssutils_logging_handler`` and
   278	``cssutils_logging_level`` (optional). For example like this:
   279	
   280	.. code:: python
   281	
   282	    >>> import logging
   283	    >>> import premailer
   284	    >>> from io import StringIO
   285	    >>> mylog = StringIO()
   286	    >>> myhandler = logging.StreamHandler(mylog)
   287	    >>> p = premailer.Premailer(
   288	    ...     cssutils_logging_handler=myhandler,
   289	    ...     cssutils_logging_level=logging.INFO
   290	    ... )
   291	    >>> result = p.transform("""
   292	    ...         <html>
   293	    ...         <style type="text/css">
   294	    ...         @keyframes foo { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }
   295	    ...         </style>
   296	    ...         <p>Hej</p>
   297	    ...         </html>
   298	    ... """)
   299	    >>> mylog.getvalue()

   306	1 HTML document but *a lot* of HTML documents. Then, the first thing you should do
   307	is avoid using the ``premailer.transform`` function because it creates a ``Premailer``
   308	class instance every time.

     1	# apischema
     2	
     3	JSON (de)serialization, *GraphQL* and JSON schema generation using Python typing.
     4	
     5	*apischema* makes your life easier when dealing with API data.
     6	
     7	## Documentation
     8	
     9	[https://wyfo.github.io/apischema/](https://wyfo.github.io/apischema/)
    10	
    11	## Install
    12	```shell
    13	pip install apischema
    14	```
    15	It requires only Python 3.6+ (and dataclasses [official backport](https://pypi.org/project/dataclasses/) for version 3.6 only)
    16	
    17	*PyPy3* is fully supported.
    18	
    19	## Why another library?
    20	
    21	(If you wonder how this differs from the *pydantic* library, see the [dedicated section of the documentation](https://wyfo.github.io/apischema/difference_with_pydantic/) — there are many differences.)
    22	
    23	This library fulfills the following goals:
    24	
    25	- stay as close as possible to the standard library (dataclasses, typing, etc.) — as a consequence we do not need plugins for editors/linters/etc.;
    26	- be adaptable, provide tools to support any types (ORM, etc.);
    27	- avoid dynamic things like using raw strings for attributes name - play nicely with your IDE.
    28	
    29	No known alternative achieves all of this, and apischema is also [faster](https://wyfo.github.io/apischema/performance_and_benchmark) than all of them.
    30	
    31	On top of that, because APIs are not only JSON, *apischema* is also a complete *GraphQL* library.
    32	
    33	## Example
    34	
    35	```python
    36	from collections.abc import Collection
    37	from dataclasses import dataclass, field
    38	from uuid import UUID, uuid4
    39	
    40	from graphql import print_schema
    41	from pytest import raises
    42	
    43	from apischema import ValidationError, deserialize, serialize
    44	from apischema.graphql import graphql_schema
    45	from apischema.json_schema import deserialization_schema
    46	
    47	
    48	# Define a schema with standard dataclasses
    49	@dataclass
    50	class Resource:
    51	    id: UUID
    52	    name: str
    53	    tags: set[str] = field(default_factory=set)
    54	
    55	
    56	# Get some data
    57	uuid = uuid4()
    58	data = {"id": str(uuid), "name": "wyfo", "tags": ["some_tag"]}
    59	# Deserialize data
    60	resource = deserialize(Resource, data)
    61	assert resource == Resource(uuid, "wyfo", {"some_tag"})
    62	# Serialize objects
    63	assert serialize(Resource, resource) == data
    64	# Validate during deserialization
    65	with raises(ValidationError) as err:  # pytest checks exception is raised
    66	    deserialize(Resource, {"id": "42", "name": "wyfo"})
    67	assert err.value.errors == [
    68	    {"loc": ["id"], "msg": "badly formed hexadecimal UUID string"}
    69	]
    70	# Generate JSON Schema
    71	assert deserialization_schema(Resource) == {
    72	    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema#",
    73	    "type": "object",
    74	    "properties": {
    75	        "id": {"type": "string", "format": "uuid"},
    76	        "name": {"type": "string"},
    77	        "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "uniqueItems": True},
    78	    },
    79	    "required": ["id", "name"],
    80	    "additionalProperties": False,
    81	}
    82	
    83	
    84	# Define GraphQL operations
    85	def resources(tags: Collection[str] | None = None) -> Collection[Resource] | None:
    86	    ...
    87	
    88	
    89	# Generate GraphQL schema
    90	schema = graphql_schema(query=[resources], id_types={UUID})
    91	schema_str = """\
    92	type Query {
    93	  resources(tags: [String!]): [Resource!]
    94	}
    95	
    96	type Resource {
    97	  id: ID!
    98	  name: String!
    99	  tags: [String!]!
   100	}
   101	"""
   102	assert print_schema(schema) == schema_str
   103	```

     1	# svgelements
     2	
     3	`svgelements` does high fidelity SVG parsing and geometric rendering. The goal is to successfully and correctly process SVG for use with any scripts that may need or want to use SVG files as geometric data.
     4	
     5	This is both facilitated by, and results in, very useful elements within the SVG spec: Path, Matrix, Angle, Length, Color, Point and other SVG and CSS Elements.      6	
     7	This project began as part of `meerK40t` which does SVG loading of files for laser cutting.    116	# Parsing
   117	
   118	The primary function of `svgelements` is to parse svg files. There are two main functions to facilitate this
   119	```python
   120	    def parse(source,
   121	              reify=True,
   122	              ppi=DEFAULT_PPI,
   123	              width=1,
   124	              height=1,
   125	              color="black",
   126	              transform=None,
   127	              context=None):
   128	```
   129	This parse function takes in values that cannot be known to the SVG but which are essential to the the rendering of the shapes. Parsing will pre-apply things like the relative translation by the viewport. It will solve the structural changes for the with the `<use>` and `<defs>`, and any items that are known SVG elements will be turned into their requisite values and parsed accordingly. So the `.fill` and `.stroke` of a `Path` will be filled in with a type of `Color` and the `.transform` of the Shape will be a type of `Matrix`. The `.values` for all the `SVGElement` will have the relevant inherited values. This permits parsing to deal with even unknown types of objects within the SVG by falling back to something akin to DOM parsing of the file. In cases of `<use>` and `<defs>` these unknown elements can still reference other. Since this structural shadow tree will be solved during the parse.
   130	
   131	`parse()` is a static function which takes a `source` file or stream of svg data to be parsed. This will return an `SVG` object which is a type of `Group`. There are several values which can be configured with other values as needed. `reify` determines whether the parsed elements in the `SVG` should have their transform matrix applied or not. This includes the effective matrix resulting from viewport.
   132	
   133	The `ppi` value defaults to `96` as this is quite common some other graphics programs use `72` and other values are permitted. Since there's nothing directly in the SVG spec setting this value and other places can vary with their value here. We can't predetermine this value. However it regulates all the relationships between physical values like a 1in by 1in `rect` to the unitless pixel values of the SVG. 
   134	
   135	The `width` and `height` values are unknown to the SVG parsing. This is the physical view size of the svg itself. This often will have little impact in the SVG rendering however sometimes things widths are set to `100%` or heights to `50%` and those are according to the spec relative to the actual view we're using. The svg has no direct access to this. If we have a `ppi` value these height and width can be set to absolute units like `6in` or any other acceptable `Length` value that can be solved with `ppi`.
   136	
   137	The `color` is the value of the `currentColor` within the SVG spec. Usually the default stroke and fill values are set but in some cases these are set to `currentColor` which is a property of the CSS outside the scope of the SVG. In this case that color needs to be provided. It will be a rare edge case.
   138	
   139	The `transform` value is typical CSS/SVG transform matrix code to be preappended to the matrix before even the viewbox. If you need to set some units or apply something to the entire svg without changing things within the CSS this value becomes important. Especially when dealing with edge cases like the difference of `transform` applied directly to the `SVG` tag itself.
   140	
   141	The `context` permits giving a context of already set values that are come from outside the current svg context, such as we would find if we had SVG files embedded into SVG files. 
   142	
   143	The second function within parsing that matters is the `.elements()` this is a function that exists on any `SVG` object and will flatten the elements yielding them in order.
   144	
   145	Here's an example parser with elements(). 
   146	
   147	```python
   148	       for element in svg.elements():
   149	            try:
   150	                if element.values['visibility'] == 'hidden':
   151	                    continue
   152	            except (KeyError, AttributeError):
   153	                pass
   154	            if isinstance(element, SVGText):
   155	                elements.append(element)
   156	            elif isinstance(element, Path):
   157	                if len(element) != 0:
   158	                    elements.append(element)
   159	            elif isinstance(element, Shape):
   160	                e = Path(element)
   161	                e.reify()  # In some cases the shape could not have reified, the path must.
   162	                if len(e) != 0:
   163	                    elements.append(e)
   164	            elif isinstance(element, SVGImage):
   165	                try:
   166	                    element.load(os.path.dirname(pathname))
   167	                    if element.image is not None:
   168	                        elements.append(element)
   169	                except OSError:
   170	                    pass  
   171	 ```
   172	
   173	Here a few things are checked. The element.values for ['visibility'] is checked if it's hidden it is not added to our flat object list. Texts are specific added. Paths are only added if they have `PathSegments` and are not completely blank. Any Shape object is converted to a Path() object and reified. Any SVGImage objects are loaded. This is a soft dependency on PIL/Pillow to load images stored within SVG. The SVG `.elements()` function can also take a conditional function that well be used to test each element before yielding it. In most cases we don't want every single type of thing an svg can produce. We might just want all the Path objects so we check for any Path and include that but also for any non-Path Shape and convert that to a path. `pathname` is an attempt to get the local directory for loading relative path images.

    99	============
   100	
   101	The oemof.solph package is part of the
   102	`Open energy modelling framework (oemof) <https://github.com/oemof/oemof>`_.
   103	This an organisational framework to bundle tools for energy (system) modelling.
   104	oemof-solph is a model generator for energy system modelling and optimisation.
   105	
   106	The ``oemof.solph`` package is very often called just ``oemof`` as it was part of the
   107	oemof meta package. Now you need to install ``oemof.solph`` instead of ``oemof``, but
   108	everything else is still the same.
   109	(Note: Since the oemof package refers to legacy versions before v0.4,
   110	it is not possible to install both, oemof and oemof.solph, at the same time.
   111	Just use ``pip install oemof.solph``.)
   112	
   113	Everybody is welcome to use and/or develop oemof.solph.
   114	Read our `contribution <https://oemof.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing.html>`_ section.
   115	
   116	Contribution is already possible on a low level by simply fixing typos in
   117	oemof's documentation or rephrasing sections which are unclear.
   118	If you want to support us that way please fork the oemof repository to your own
   119	github account and make changes as described in the `github guidelines <https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/hello-world>`_
   120

    17	This library is targeting to provide only an IoC-container but make it really useful. If you are tired manually passing objects to create others objects which are only used to create more objects - we have a solution. Not all project require an IoC-container, but check what we have.

    24	* **Modular providers**. Instead of creating lots of separate functions or contrariwise a big single class, you can split your factories into several classes, which makes them simpler reusable.
    25	* **Clean dependencies**. You do not need to add custom markers to the code of dependencies so to allow library to see them. All customization is done within providers code and only borders of scopes have to deal with library API.
    26	* **Simple API**. You need minimum of objects to start using library. You can easily integrate it with your task framework, examples provided.
    27	* **Speed**. It is fast enough so you not to worry about. It is even faster than many of the analogs.
    28	
    29	See more in [technical requirements](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/requirements/technical.html)
    30	
    31	### Quickstart
    32	
    33	1. Install dishka
    34	
    35	```shell
    36	pip install dishka
    37	```
    38	
    39	2. Create `Provider` instance. It is only used to setup all factories providing your objects.
    40	
    41	```python
    42	from dishka import Provider
    43	
    44	provider = Provider()
    45	```
    46	
    47	3. Register functions which provide dependencies. Do not forget to place correct typehints for parameters and result. We use `scope=Scope.APP` for dependencies which ar created only once in applicaiton lifetime, and `scope=Scope.REQUEST` for those which should be recreated for each processing request/event/etc.
    48	
    49	```python
    50	from dishka import Provider, Scope
    51	
    52	def get_a() -> A:
    53	   return A()
    54	
    55	def get_b(a: A) -> B:
    56	   return B(a)
    57	
    58	provider = Provider()
    59	provider.provide(get_a, scope=Scope.APP)
    60	provider.provide(get_b, scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    61	```
    62	
    63	This can be also rewritten using classes:
    64	
    65	```python
    66	from dishka import provide, Provider, Scope
    67	
    68	class MyProvider(Provider):
    69	  @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
    70	  def get_a(self) -> A:
    71	     return A()
    72	  
    73	  @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    74	  def get_b(self, a: A) -> B:
    75	     return B(a)
    76	
    77	provider = MyProvider()
    78	```
    79	
    80	4. Create Container instance passing providers, and step into `APP` scope. Container holds dependencies cache and is used to retrieve them. Here, you can use `.get` method to access APP-scoped dependencies:
    81	
    82	```python
    83	from dishka import make_container
    84	container = make_container(provider)  # it has Scope.APP
    85	a = container.get(A)  # `A` has Scope.APP, so it is accessible here
    86	```
    87	
    88	5. You can enter and exit `REQUEST` scope multiple times after that:
    89	
    90	```python
    91	from dishka import make_container
    92	container = make_container(provider)
    93	with container() as request_container:
    94	    b = request_container.get(B)  # `B` has Scope.REQUEST
    95	    a = request_container.get(A)  # `A` is accessible here too
    96	
    97	with container() as request_container:
    98	    b = request_container.get(B)  # another instance of `B`
    99	    a = request_container.get(A)  # the same instance of `A`
   100	```
   101	
   102	6. Close container in the end:
   103	
   104	```python
   105	container.close()
   106	```
   107	
   108	7. If you are using supported framework add decorators and middleware for it.
   109	
   110	```python
   111	from dishka.integrations.fastapi import (
   112	    FromDishka, inject, setup_dishka,
   113	)
   114	
   115	@router.get("/")
   116	@inject
   117	async def index(a: FromDishka[A]) -> str:
   118	    ...
   119	
   120	...
   121	
   122	setup_dishka(container, app)
   123	```
   124	
   125	### Concepts
   126	
   127	**Dependency** is what you need for some part of your code to work. They are just object which you do not create in place and probably want to replace some day. At least for tests.
   128	Some of them can live while you application is running, others are destroyed and created on each request. Dependencies can depend on other objects, which are their dependencies.
   129	
   130	**Scope** is a lifespan of a dependency. Standard scopes are (without skipped ones):
   131	
   132	  `APP` -> `REQUEST` -> `ACTION` -> `STEP`.
   133	
   134	You decide when to enter and exit them, but it is done one by one. You set a scope for your dependency when you configure how to create it. If the same dependency is requested multiple time within one scope without leaving it, then by default the same instance is returned.
   135	
   136	If you are developing web application, you would enter `APP` scope on startup, and you would `REQUEST` scope in each HTTP-request.
   137	
   138	You can provide your own Scopes class if you are not satisfied with standard flow.
   139	
   140	**Container** is what you use to get your dependency. You just call `.get(SomeType)` and it finds a way to get you an instance of that type. It does not create things itself, but manages their lifecycle and caches. It delegates objects creation to providers which are passed during creation.
   141	
   142	**Provider** is a collection of functions which really provide some objects. 
   143	Provider itself is a class with some attributes and methods. Each of them is either result of `provide`, `alias` or `decorate`. They can be used as provider methods, functions to assign attributes or method decorators.
   144	
   145	`@provide` can be used as a decorator for some method. This method will be called when corresponding dependency has to be created. Name of the method is not important: just check that it is different form other `Provider` attributes. Type hints do matter: they show what this method creates and what does it require. All method parameters are treated as other dependencies and created using container.
   146	
   147	If `provide` is used with some class then that class itself is treated as a factory (`__init__` is analyzed for parameters). But do not forget to assing that call to some attribute otherwise it will be ignored.
   148	
   149	**Component** - is an isolated group of providers within the same container identified by a string. When dependency is requested it is searched only within the same component as its dependant, unless it is declared explicitly.
   150	
   151	This allows you to have multiple parts of application build separately without need to think if the use same types.
   152	
   153	### Tips
   154	
   155	* Add method and mark it with `@provide` decorator. It can be sync or async method returning some value.
   156	
   157	    ```python
   158	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   159	        @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   160	        def get_a(self) -> A:
   161	            return A()
   162	    ```
   163	* Want some finalization when exiting the scope? Make that method generator:
   164	
   165	    ```python
   166	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   167	        @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   168	        def get_a(self) -> Iterable[A]:
   169	            a = A()
   170	            yield a
   171	            a.close()
   172	    ```
   173	* Do not have any specific logic and just want to create class using its `__init__`? then add a provider attribute using `provide` as function passing that class. 
   174	
   175	    ```python 
   176	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   177	        a = provide(A, scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   178	    ```
   179	* Want to create a child class instance when parent is requested? add a `source` attribute to `provide` function with a parent class while passing child as a first parameter
   180	
   181	    ```python 
   182	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   183	        a = provide(source=AChild, scope=Scope.REQUEST, provides=A)
   184	    ```
   185	* Having multiple interfaces which can be created as a same class? Use `AnyOf`:
   186	
   187	    ```python
   188	    from dishka import AnyOf
   189	
   190	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   191	        @provide
   192	        def p(self) -> AnyOf[A, AProtocol]:
   193	            return A()
   194	    ```
   195	
   196	    Use alias if you want to add them in another `Provider`:
   197	
   198	    ```python
   199	    class MyProvider2(Provider):
   200	        p = alias(source=A, provides=AProtocol)
   201	    ```
   202	
   203	    In both cases it works the same way as
   204	
   205	    ```python
   206	    class MyProvider2(Provider):
   207	        @provide(scope=<Scope of A>)
   208	        def p(self, a: A) -> AProtocol:
   209	            return a
   210	    ```
   211	
   212	
   213	* Want to apply decorator pattern and do not want to alter existing provide method? Use `decorate`. It will construct object using earlie defined provider and then pass it to your decorator before returning from the container.
   214	
   215	  ```python
   216	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   217	        @decorate
   218	        def decorate_a(self, a: A) -> A:
   219	            return ADecorator(a)
   220	   ```
   221	  Decorator function can also have additional parameters.
   222	
   223	* Want to go `async`? Make provide methods asynchronous. Create async container. Use `async with` and await `get` calls:
   224	
   225	```python
   226	class MyProvider(Provider):
   227	   @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
   228	   async def get_a(self) -> A:
   229	      return A()
   230	
   231	container = make_async_container(MyProvider())
   232	a = await container.get(A)
   233	```
   234	
   235	* Having some data connected with scope which you want to use when solving dependencies? Set it when entering scope. These classes can be used as parameters of your `provide` methods. But you need to specify them in provider as retrieved form context.
   236	
   237	```python
   238	from dishka import from_context, Provider, provide, Scope
   239	
   240	class MyProvider(Provider):
   241	    scope = Scope.REQUEST
   242	
   243	    app = from_context(provides=App, scope=Scope.APP)
   244	    request = from_context(provides=RequestClass)
   245	
   246	    @provide
   247	    def get_a(self, request: RequestClass, app: App) -> A:
   248	        ...
   249	
   250	container = make_container(MyProvider(), context={App: app})
   251	with container(context={RequestClass: request_instance}) as request_container:
   252	    pass
   253	```
   254	
   255	* Having to many dependencies? Or maybe want to replace only part of them in tests keeping others? Create multiple `Provider` classes
   256	
   257	```python
   258	container = make_container(MyProvider(), OtherProvider())
   259	```
   260	
   261	* Tired of providing `scope==` for each depedency? Set it inside your `Provider` class and all dependencies with no scope will use it.
   262	
   263	```python
   264	class MyProvider(Provider):
   265	   scope = Scope.APP
   266	
   267	   @provide
   268	   async def get_a(self) -> A:
   269	      return A()
   270	```

   105	## Features
   106	### Structure parsing
   107	Write simple C-like structures and use them to parse binary data, as can be seen in the examples.
   108	
   109	### Type parsing
   110	Aside from loading structure definitions, any of the supported types can be used individually for parsing data. For example, the following is all supported:
   111	
   112	```python
   113	from dissect import cstruct
   114	cs = cstruct.cstruct()
   115	# Default endianness is LE, but can be configured using a kwarg or setting the attribute
   116	# e.g. cstruct.cstruct(endian='>') or cs.endian = '>'
   117	assert cs.uint32(b'\x05\x00\x00\x00') == 5
   118	assert cs.uint24[2](b'\x01\x00\x00\x02\x00\x00') == [1, 2]  # You can also parse arrays using list indexing
   119	assert cs.char[None](b'hello world!\x00') == b'hello world!'  # A list index of None means null terminated
   120	```
   121	
   122	### Unions and nested structures
   123	Unions and nested structures are supported, both anonymous and named.
   124

   126	cdef = """
   127	struct test_union {
   128	    char magic[4];
   129	    union {
   130	        struct {
   131	            uint32 a;
   132	            uint32 b;
   133	        } a;
   134	        struct {
   135	            char   b[8];
   136	        } b;
   137	    } c;
   138	};
   139	
   140	struct test_anonymous {
   141	    char magic[4];
   142	    struct {
   143	        uint32 a;
   144	        uint32 b;
   145	    };
   146	    struct {
   147	        char   c[8];
   148	    };
   149	};
   150	"""
   151	c = cstruct.cstruct()
   152	c.load(cdef)
   153

   155	
   156	a = c.test_union(b'ohaideadbeef')
   157	assert a.magic == b'ohai'
   158	assert a.c.a.a == 0x64616564
   159	assert a.c.a.b == 0x66656562
   160	assert a.c.b.b == b'deadbeef'
   161	
   162	assert a.dumps() == b'ohaideadbeef'

    18	
    19	`Hazelcast <https://hazelcast.org/>`__ is an open-source distributed
    20	in-memory data store and computation platform that provides a wide
    21	variety of distributed data structures and concurrency primitives.
    22	
    23	Hazelcast Python client is a way to communicate to Hazelcast IMDG
    24	clusters and access the cluster data. The client provides a
    25	Future-based asynchronous API suitable for wide ranges of use cases.
    26	
    27	Installation
    28	------------
    29	
    30	Hazelcast
    31	~~~~~~~~~
    32	
    33	Hazelcast Python client requires a working Hazelcast IMDG cluster to
    34	run. This cluster handles the storage and manipulation of the user data.
    35	
    36	A Hazelcast IMDG cluster consists of one or more cluster members. These
    37	members generally run on multiple virtual or physical machines and are
    38	connected to each other via the network. Any data put on the cluster is
    39	partitioned to multiple members transparent to the user. It is therefore
    40	very easy to scale the system by adding new members as the data grows.
    41	Hazelcast IMDG cluster also offers resilience. Should any hardware or
    42	software problem causes a crash to any member, the data on that member
    43	is recovered from backups and the cluster continues to operate without
    44	any downtime.
    45	
    46	The quickest way to start a single member cluster for development
    47	purposes is to use our `Docker
    48	images <https://hub.docker.com/r/hazelcast/hazelcast/>`__.
    49	
    50	.. code:: bash
    51	
    52	   docker run -p 5701:5701 hazelcast/hazelcast:4.1
    53	
    54	You can also use our ZIP or TAR
    55	`distributions <https://hazelcast.org/imdg/download/archives/#hazelcast-imdg>`__.
    56	Once you have downloaded, you can start the Hazelcast member using
    57	the ``bin/start.sh`` script.
    58	
    59	Client
    60	~~~~~~
    61	
    62	.. code:: bash
    63	
    64	   pip install hazelcast-python-client
    65	
    66	Overview
    67	--------
    68	
    69	Usage
    70	~~~~~
    71	
    72	.. code:: python
    73	
    74	    import hazelcast
    75	
    76	    # Connect to Hazelcast cluster.
    77	    client = hazelcast.HazelcastClient()
    78	
    79	    # Get or create the "distributed-map" on the cluster.
    80	    distributed_map = client.get_map("distributed-map")
    81	
    82	    # Put "key", "value" pair into the "distributed-map" and wait for
    83	    # the request to complete.
    84	    distributed_map.set("key", "value").result()
    85	
    86	    # Try to get the value associated with the given key from the cluster
    87	    # and attach a callback to be executed once the response for the
    88	    # get request is received. Note that, the set request above was
    89	    # blocking since it calls ".result()" on the returned Future, whereas
    90	    # the get request below is non-blocking.
    91	    get_future = distributed_map.get("key")
    92	    get_future.add_done_callback(lambda future: print(future.result()))
    93	
    94	    # Do other operations. The operations below won't wait for
    95	    # the get request above to complete.
    96	
    97	    print("Map size:", distributed_map.size().result())
    98	
    99	    # Shutdown the client.
   100	    client.shutdown()
   101	
   102	
   103	If you are using Hazelcast IMDG and the Python client on the same
   104	machine, the default configuration should work out-of-the-box. However,
   105	you may need to configure the client to connect to cluster nodes that
   106	are running on different machines or to customize client properties.

   117	        cluster_members=[

   119	            "10.90.0.3:5701",
   120	        ],
   121	        lifecycle_listeners=[

   123	        ]
   124	    )

   133	Features
   134	--------
   135	
   136	-  Distributed, partitioned and queryable in-memory key-value store
   137	   implementation, called **Map**
   138	-  Eventually consistent cache implementation to store a subset of the
   139	   Map data locally in the memory of the client, called **Near Cache**
   140	-  Additional data structures and simple messaging constructs such as
   141	   **Set**, **MultiMap**, **Queue**, **Topic**
   142	-  Cluster-wide unique ID generator, called **FlakeIdGenerator**
   143	-  Distributed, CRDT based counter, called **PNCounter**
   144	-  Distributed concurrency primitives from CP Subsystem such as

import asyncio

from asyncstdlib.functools import cached_property


class Foo:
    @cached_property
    async def bar(self) -> int:
        await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.1))
        value = random.randrange(1, 100)
        print("Foo.bar ->", value)
        return value


async def demo():
    foo = Foo()
    results = await asyncio.gather(foo.bar, foo.bar, foo.bar)
    print(*results)
    print(await foo.bar)

    asyncio.run(demo())
```

The above script outputs something like:

```plain
% python demo.py
Foo.bar -> 90
Foo.bar -> 34
Foo.bar -> 76
34 76 90
76
```

I'd like to see a decorator where only the _first_ task determines the value, and any concurrent access before the first task completes having to wait for the result to have been computed. This could be achieved if the decorator first assigned an intermediary object to the instance `__dict__`, one that holds an `asyncio.Future()` instance for subsequent (concurrent) calls. Here is what that could look like (using Python 3.12 type annotation syntax for generics):

```python
class _FutureCachedValue[I, T]:
    __slots__ = ("_get_attribute", "_instance", "_fut")

    _fut: asyncio.Future[T]

    def __init__(
        self, get_attribute: Callable[[I], Coroutine[Any, Any, T]], instance: I
    ):
        self._get_attribute = get_attribute
        self._instance = instance

    def __await__(self) -> Generator[Any, Any, T]:
        try:
            fut = self._fut
        except AttributeError:
            # _fut is not yet set, this is the first accessing task
            return self._fill_future().__await__()
        else:
            # this is another, concurrent task, have it wait for the cache to be filled
            return fut.__await__()

    async def _fill_future(self) -> T:
        self._fut = asyncio.Future()
        try:
            value = await self._get_attribute(self._instance)
        except Exception as e:
            # share the exception across all waiting tasks
            self._fut.set_exception(e)
            # but allow a new task to re-attempt to fetch the value
            del self._fut
            raise
        self._fut.set_result(value)
        return value
```

<issue_description>
aiohttp swallows asyncio.CancelledError during connection timeout
### Describe the bug

There is a race condition in code that handles connection timeout. If you call `cancel` on a task that is currently pending in `create_connection` and connection timeout was already fired then `asyncio.CancelledError` is not propagated and you get `asyncio.TimeoutError` instead. The main problem is in how timeouts are handled in [async_timeout](https://github.com/aio-libs/async-timeout/blob/v3.0.1/async_timeout/__init__.py#L88) package. When exitting the context manager after timeout had passed all `CancelledError` exceptions are swallowed and `TimeoutError` is raised instead. Unfortunately this is true also if you explicitly cancel the task yourself.

The main problem is that you cannot cancel a task that is using aiohttp because you never know if `CancelledError` will be raised.

### To Reproduce
**EDIT: THIS REPRODUCER DOES NOT SHOW THE BEHAVIOUR CORRECTLY - PLEASE REFER TO COMMENTS BELLOW!**
```python
import asyncio
from async_timeout import timeout


async def test_task():
    with timeout(1):
        await asyncio.sleep(10)


async def main():
    t = asyncio.create_task(test_task())
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    t.cancel()
    try:
        await t
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print("Raised TimeoutError")
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("Raised CancelledError")

asyncio.run(main())
```

### Expected behavior

`asyncio.CancelledError` should never be suppressed when you cancel the task explicitly.

    16	Usage example
    17	-------------
    18	
    19	
    20	The context manager is useful in cases when you want to apply timeout
    21	logic around block of code or in cases when ``asyncio.wait_for()`` is
    22	not suitable. Also it's much faster than ``asyncio.wait_for()``
    23	because ``timeout`` doesn't create a new task.
    24	
    25	The ``timeout(delay, *, loop=None)`` call returns a context manager
    26	that cancels a block on *timeout* expiring::
    27	
    28	   async with timeout(1.5):
    29	       await inner()
    30	
    31	1. If ``inner()`` is executed faster than in ``1.5`` seconds nothing
    32	   happens.
    33	2. Otherwise ``inner()`` is cancelled internally by sending
    34	   ``asyncio.CancelledError`` into but ``asyncio.TimeoutError`` is
    35	   raised outside of context manager scope.
    36	
    37	*timeout* parameter could be ``None`` for skipping timeout functionality.
    38	
    39	
    40	Alternatively, ``timeout_at(when)`` can be used for scheduling
    41	at the absolute time::
    42	
    43	   loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    44	   now = loop.time()
    45	
    46	   async with timeout_at(now + 1.5):
    47	       await inner()
    48	
    49	
    50	Please note: it is not POSIX time but a time with
    51	undefined starting base, e.g. the time of the system power on.
    52	
    53	
    54	Context manager has ``.expired`` property for check if timeout happens
    55	exactly in context manager::
    56	
    57	   async with timeout(1.5) as cm:
    58	       await inner()
    59	   print(cm.expired)
    60	
    61	The property is ``True`` if ``inner()`` execution is cancelled by
    62	timeout context manager.

    64	If ``inner()`` call explicitly raises ``TimeoutError`` ``cm.expired``

    17	
    18	
    19	MontePy is the most user friendly Python library for reading, editing, and writing MCNP input files. 
    20	
    21	## Installing
    22	
    23	Simply run:
    24	
    25	```
    26	pip install montepy
    27	```
    28	
    29	For more complicated setups
    30	see the [Installing section in the user guide](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/starting.html#installing).
    31	
    32	
    33	## User Documentation
    34	
    35	MontePy has a website [documenting how to work with MCNP in python with MontePy](https://www.montepy.org/). 
    36	The website contains a user's guide for getting started, 
    37	a developer's guide covering the design and approach of MontePy,
    38	instructions for contributing, 
    39	and the Python API documentation.
    40	
    41	## Features
    42		
    43	* Handles almost all MCNP input syntax.
    44	* Parses Cells, Surfaces, Materials, and Transforms very well.	
    45	* Can parse all surface types except macrobody facets ([Issue #354](https://github.com/idaholab/MontePy/issues/354)).
    46	* Can read and write out all other MCNP inputs, even if it doesn't not understand them	
    47	* Attempts to write out the MCNP problem verbatim, even matching the original user formatting. (See some of the [open issues](https://github.com/idaholab/MontePy/issues).)
    48	* Can quickly [access cells, surfaces, and materials by their numbers](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/starting.html#collections-are-accessible-by-number). For example: `cell = problem.cells[105]`.
    49	* Can quickly update cell parameters, [such as importances](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/starting.html#setting-cell-importances). For example `cell.importance.neutron = 2.0`.
    50	* Can easily [create universes, and fill other cells with universes](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/starting.html#universes).
    51	* Currently has over 550 test cases.
    52	
    53	 
    54	Here is a quick example showing multiple tasks in MontePy:
    55	
    56	
    57	``` python
    58	import montepy
    59	# read in file
    60	problem = montepy.read_input("tests/inputs/test.imcnp")
    61	  
    62	# set photon importance for multiple cells
    63	importances = {1: 0.005,
    64	   2: 0.1,
    65	   3: 1.0,
    66	   99: 1.235
    67	}
    68	for cell_num, importance in importances.items():
    69	   problem.cells[cell_num].importance.photon = importance
    70	
    71	#create a universe and fill another cell with it
    72	universe = montepy.Universe(123)
    73	problem.universes.append(universe)
    74	# add all cells with numbers between 1 and 4
    75	universe.claim(problem.cells[1:5])
    76	# fill cell 99 with universe 123
    77	problem.cells[99].fill.universe = universe
    78	
    79	# update all surfaces numbers by adding 1000 to them
    80	for surface in problem.surfaces:
    81	   surface.number += 1000
    82	# all cells using these surfaces will be automatically updated as well
    83	
    84	#write out an updated file
    85	problem.write_problem("foo_update.imcnp")
    86	```
    87	
    88	For more examples see the [getting started guide](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/starting.html).
    89	
    90	## Limitations
    91	
    92	Here a few of the known bugs and limitations:
    93	
    94		
    95	* Cannot handle vertical input mode.
    96	* Does not support editing tallies in a user-friendly way.
    97	* Does not support editing source definition in a user-friendly way.
    98	* Cannot parse all valid material definitions. There is a known bug ([#182](https://github.com/idaholab/MontePy/issues/182)) that MontePy can only parse materials where all
    99	    keyword-value pairs show up after the nuclide definitions. For example:
   100	   * `M1 1001.80c 1.0 plib=80p` can be parsed.
   101	   * `M1 plib=80p 1001.80c 1.0` cannot be parsed; despite it being a valid input.
   102	
   103	## Current Development Priorities
   104	
   105	Here are the rough development priorities for adding new features to MontePy:
   106	
   107	#. Redesign the `Material` interface to be more user friendly.
   108	#. Implement support for tallies.
   109	#. Implement support for source definitions.
   110	
   111	If you have a specific feature priority that you would be willing to collaborate on you can open an issue or email us at [mgale@montepy.org](mailto:mgale@montepy.org). 
   112	
   113	## Alternatives
   114	
   115	There are some python packages that offer some of the same features as MontePy,
   116	    but don't offer the same level of robustness, ease of installation, and user friendliness.
   117	
   118	
   119	Many of the competitors do not offer the robustness that MontePy does because,
   120	    they do not utilize context-free parsing (as of 2024). 
   121	These packages are:
   122	
   123	* [pyMCNP](https://github.com/FSIBT/PyMCNP)
   124	
   125	* [MCNP-Input-Reader](https://github.com/ENEA-Fusion-Neutronics/MCNP-Input-Reader)
   126	
   127	* [numjuggler](https://github.com/inr-kit/numjuggler)
   128	
   129	The only other libraries that do utilize context-free parsing that we are aware of are:
   130	* [MCNPy](https://github.rpi.edu/NuCoMP/mcnpy)
   131	* [mckit](https://github.com/MC-kit/mckit) 
   132	
   133	MontePy differs from MCNPy by being:
   134	* On PyPI, and can be installed via pip.
   135	* Only requires a python interpreter, and not a Java virtual machine. 
   136	* Allowing contributions from anyone with a public GitHub account
   137	
   138	MontePy differs from mckit by being:
   139	* thoroughly documented
   140	* Object-Oriented 
   141	
   142	
   143	For only writing, or templating an input file there are also some great tools out there. 
   144	These packages don't provide the same functionality as MontePy inherently,
   145	    but could be the right tool for the job depending on the user's needs.
   146	
   147	* [Workflow and Template Toolkit for Simulation (WATTS)](https://github.com/watts-dev/watts)
   148	* [Advanced Reactor Modeling Interface (ARMI)](https://github.com/terrapower/armi)
   149	
   150	Another honorable mention that doesn't replicate the features of MontePy,
   151	    but could be a great supplement to MontePy for defining materials, performing activations, etc.
   152	    is [PyNE --- the Nuclear Engineering Toolkit](https://pyne.io/).
   153		
   154	## Bugs, Requests and Development
   155	
   156	So MontePy doesn't do what you want? 
   157	Add an issue here with the "feature request" tag. 
   158	The system is very modular and you should be able to develop it pretty quickly.
   159	Read the [developer's guide](https://www.montepy.org/en/stable/developing.html) for more details.
   160	If you have any questions feel free to ask [@micahgale](mailto:mgale@montepy.org).
   161	
   162	## Citation

   164	For citing MontePy in a publication a [Journal of Open Source Software](https://joss.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) article is under review.

     9	xarray data creation made easy by dataclass
    10	
    11	## Overview
    12	
    13	xarray-dataclasses is a Python package that makes it easy to create [xarray]'s DataArray and Dataset objects that are "typed" (i.e. fixed dimensions, data type, coordinates, attributes, and name) using [the Python's dataclass]:
    14	
    15	```python
    16	from dataclasses import dataclass
    17	from typing import Literal
    18	from xarray_dataclasses import AsDataArray, Coord, Data
    19	
    20	
    21	X = Literal["x"]
    22	Y = Literal["y"]
    23	
    24	
    25	@dataclass
    26	class Image(AsDataArray):
    27	    """2D image as DataArray."""
    28	
    29	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
    30	    x: Coord[X, int] = 0
    31	    y: Coord[Y, int] = 0
    32	```
    33	
    34	### Features
    35	
    36	- Typed DataArray or Dataset objects can easily be created:
    37	  ```python
    38	  image = Image.new([[0, 1], [2, 3]], [0, 1], [0, 1])
    39	  ```
    40	- NumPy-like filled-data creation is also available:
    41	  ```python
    42	  image = Image.zeros([2, 2], x=[0, 1], y=[0, 1])
    43	  ```
    44	- Support for features by [the Python's dataclass] (`field`, `__post_init__`, ...).
    45	- Support for static type check by [Pyright].
    46	
    47	### Installation
    48	
    49	```shell
    50	pip install xarray-dataclasses
    51	```
    52	
    53	## Basic usage
    54	
    55	xarray-dataclasses uses [the Python's dataclass].
    56	Data (or data variables), coordinates, attributes, and a name of DataArray or Dataset objects will be defined as dataclass fields by special type hints (`Data`, `Coord`, `Attr`, `Name`), respectively.
    57	Note that the following code is supposed in the examples below.
    58	
    59	```python
    60	from dataclasses import dataclass
    61	from typing import Literal
    62	from xarray_dataclasses import AsDataArray, AsDataset
    63	from xarray_dataclasses import Attr, Coord, Data, Name
    64	
    65	
    66	X = Literal["x"]
    67	Y = Literal["y"]
    68	```
    69	
    70	### Data field
    71	
    72	Data field is a field whose value will become the data of a DataArray object or a data variable of a Dataset object.
    73	The type hint `Data[TDims, TDtype]` fixes the dimensions and the data type of the object.
    74	Here are some examples of how to specify them.
    75	
    76	Type hint | Inferred dimensions
    77	--- | ---
    78	`Data[tuple[()], ...]` | `()`
    79	`Data[Literal["x"], ...]` | `("x",)`
    80	`Data[tuple[Literal["x"]], ...]` | `("x",)`
    81	`Data[tuple[Literal["x"], Literal["y"]], ...]` | `("x", "y")`
    82	
    83	Type hint | Inferred data type
    84	--- | ---
    85	`Data[..., Any]` | `None`
    86	`Data[..., None]` | `None`
    87	`Data[..., float]` | `numpy.dtype("float64")`
    88	`Data[..., numpy.float128]` | `numpy.dtype("float128")`
    89	`Data[..., Literal["datetime64[ns]"]]` | `numpy.dtype("<M8[ns]")`
    90	
    91	### Coordinate field
    92	
    93	Coordinate field is a field whose value will become a coordinate of a DataArray or a Dataset object.
    94	The type hint `Coord[TDims, TDtype]` fixes the dimensions and the data type of the object.
    95	
    96	### Attribute field
    97	
    98	Attribute field is a field whose value will become an attribute of a DataArray or a Dataset object.
    99	The type hint `Attr[TAttr]` specifies the type of the value, which is used only for static type check.
   100	
   101	### Name field
   102	
   103	Name field is a field whose value will become the name of a DataArray object.
   104	The type hint `Name[TName]` specifies the type of the value, which is used only for static type check.
   105	
   106	### DataArray class
   107	
   108	DataArray class is a dataclass that defines typed DataArray specifications.
   109	Exactly one data field is allowed in a DataArray class.
   110	The second and subsequent data fields are just ignored in DataArray creation.
   111	
   112	```python
   113	@dataclass
   114	class Image(AsDataArray):
   115	    """2D image as DataArray."""
   116	
   117	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   118	    x: Coord[X, int] = 0
   119	    y: Coord[Y, int] = 0
   120	    units: Attr[str] = "cd / m^2"
   121	    name: Name[str] = "luminance"
   122	```
   123	
   124	A DataArray object will be created by a class method `new()`:
   125	
   126	```python
   127	Image.new([[0, 1], [2, 3]], x=[0, 1], y=[0, 1])
   128	
   129	<xarray.DataArray "luminance" (x: 2, y: 2)>
   130	array([[0., 1.],
   131	       [2., 3.]])
   132	Coordinates:
   133	  * x        (x) int64 0 1
   134	  * y        (y) int64 0 1
   135	Attributes:
   136	    units:    cd / m^2
   137	```
   138	
   139	NumPy-like class methods (`zeros()`, `ones()`, ...) are also available:
   140	
   141	```python
   142	Image.ones((3, 3))
   143	
   144	<xarray.DataArray "luminance" (x: 3, y: 3)>
   145	array([[1., 1., 1.],
   146	       [1., 1., 1.],
   147	       [1., 1., 1.]])
   148	Coordinates:
   149	  * x        (x) int64 0 0 0
   150	  * y        (y) int64 0 0 0
   151	Attributes:
   152	    units:    cd / m^2
   153	```
   154	
   155	### Dataset class
   156	
   157	Dataset class is a dataclass that defines typed Dataset specifications.
   158	Multiple data fields are allowed to define the data variables of the object.
   159	
   160	```python
   161	@dataclass
   162	class ColorImage(AsDataset):
   163	    """2D color image as Dataset."""
   164	
   165	    red: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   166	    green: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   167	    blue: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   168	    x: Coord[X, int] = 0
   169	    y: Coord[Y, int] = 0
   170	    units: Attr[str] = "cd / m^2"
   171	```
   172	
   173	A Dataset object will be created by a class method `new()`:
   174	
   175	```python
   176	ColorImage.new(
   177	    [[0, 0], [0, 0]],  # red
   178	    [[1, 1], [1, 1]],  # green
   179	    [[2, 2], [2, 2]],  # blue
   180	)
   181	
   182	<xarray.Dataset>
   183	Dimensions:  (x: 2, y: 2)
   184	Coordinates:
   185	  * x        (x) int64 0 0
   186	  * y        (y) int64 0 0
   187	Data variables:
   188	    red      (x, y) float64 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0
   189	    green    (x, y) float64 1.0 1.0 1.0 1.0
   190	    blue     (x, y) float64 2.0 2.0 2.0 2.0
   191	Attributes:
   192	    units:    cd / m^2
   193	```
   194	
   195	## Advanced usage
   196	
   197	### Coordof and Dataof type hints
   198	
   199	xarray-dataclasses provides advanced type hints, `Coordof` and `Dataof`.
   200	Unlike `Data` and `Coord`, they specify a dataclass that defines a DataArray class.
   201	This is useful when users want to add metadata to dimensions for [plotting].
   202	For example:
   203	
   204	```python
   205	from xarray_dataclasses import Coordof
   206	
   207	
   208	@dataclass
   209	class XAxis:
   210	    data: Data[X, int]
   211	    long_name: Attr[str] = "x axis"
   212	    units: Attr[str] = "pixel"
   213	
   214	
   215	@dataclass
   216	class YAxis:
   217	    data: Data[Y, int]
   218	    long_name: Attr[str] = "y axis"
   219	    units: Attr[str] = "pixel"
   220	
   221	
   222	@dataclass
   223	class Image(AsDataArray):
   224	    """2D image as DataArray."""
   225	
   226	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   227	    x: Coordof[XAxis] = 0
   228	    y: Coordof[YAxis] = 0
   229	```
   230	
   231	### General data variable names in Dataset creation
   232	
   233	Due to the limitation of Python's parameter names, it is not possible to define data variable names that contain white spaces, for example.
   234	In such cases, please define DataArray classes of each data variable so that they have name fields and specify them by `Dataof` in a Dataset class.
   235	Then the values of the name fields will be used as data variable names.
   236	For example:
   237	
   238	```python
   239	@dataclass
   240	class Red:
   241	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   242	    name: Name[str] = "Red image"
   243	
   244	
   245	@dataclass
   246	class Green:
   247	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   248	    name: Name[str] = "Green image"
   249	
   250	
   251	@dataclass
   252	class Blue:
   253	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   254	    name: Name[str] = "Blue image"
   255	
   256	
   257	@dataclass
   258	class ColorImage(AsDataset):
   259	    """2D color image as Dataset."""
   260	
   261	    red: Dataof[Red]
   262	    green: Dataof[Green]
   263	    blue: Dataof[Blue]
   264	```
   265	
   266	```python
   267	ColorImage.new(
   268	    [[0, 0], [0, 0]],
   269	    [[1, 1], [1, 1]],
   270	    [[2, 2], [2, 2]],
   271	)
   272	
   273	<xarray.Dataset>
   274	Dimensions:      (x: 2, y: 2)
   275	Dimensions without coordinates: x, y
   276	Data variables:
   277	    Red image    (x, y) float64 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0
   278	    Green image  (x, y) float64 1.0 1.0 1.0 1.0
   279	    Blue image   (x, y) float64 2.0 2.0 2.0 2.0
   280	```
   281	
   282	### Customization of DataArray or Dataset creation
   283	
   284	For customization, users can add a special class attribute, `__dataoptions__`, to a DataArray or Dataset class.
   285	A custom factory for DataArray or Dataset creation is only supported in the current implementation.
   286	
   287	
   288	```python
   289	import xarray as xr
   290	from xarray_dataclasses import DataOptions
   291	
   292	
   293	class Custom(xr.DataArray):
   294	    """Custom DataArray."""
   295	
   296	    __slots__ = ()
   297	
   298	    def custom_method(self) -> bool:
   299	        """Custom method."""
   300	        return True
   301	
   302	
   303	@dataclass
   304	class Image(AsDataArray):
   305	    """2D image as DataArray."""
   306	
   307	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   308	    x: Coord[X, int] = 0
   309	    y: Coord[Y, int] = 0
   310	
   311	    __dataoptions__ = DataOptions(Custom)
   312	
   313	
   314	image = Image.ones([3, 3])
   315	isinstance(image, Custom)  # True
   316	image.custom_method()  # True
   317	```
   318	
   319	### DataArray and Dataset creation without shorthands
   320	
   321	xarray-dataclasses provides functions, `asdataarray` and `asdataset`.
   322	This is useful when users do not want to inherit the mix-in class (`AsDataArray` or `AsDataset`) in a DataArray or Dataset dataclass.
   323	For example:
   324	
   325	```python
   326	from xarray_dataclasses import asdataarray
   327	
   328	
   329	@dataclass
   330	class Image:
   331	    """2D image as DataArray."""
   332	
   333	    data: Data[tuple[X, Y], float]
   334	    x: Coord[X, int] = 0
   335	    y: Coord[Y, int] = 0
   336	
   337	
   338	image = asdataarray(Image([[0, 1], [2, 3]], [0, 1], [0, 1]))
   339	```
   340

   109	by (a) guessing where to start using `__file__` or the working directory
   110	-- allowing this to work in non-file contexts such as IPython notebooks
   111	and the REPL, and then (b) walking up the directory tree looking for the
   112	specified file -- called `.env` by default.

   114	```python

   128	>>> from dotenv import dotenv_values
   129	>>> filelike = StringIO('SPAM=EGGS\n')
   130	>>> filelike.seek(0)
   131	>>> parsed = dotenv_values(stream=filelike)
   132	>>> parsed['SPAM']
   133	'EGGS'
   134	```

   136	The returned value is dictionary with key-value pairs.

<issue_description>
Setting explicit Content-Type header in addition to json body results in comma-delimited Content-Type
### Describe the bug

When passing a JSON payload to a response object as `json=...`, the content-type is automatically set to `application/json`.
Attempting to set Content-Type explicitly results in a malformed header, with the content-type values comma-separated.

### Additional context

Explicitly setting `Content-Type: application/json` causes this, but is easily rectified by removing that value and relying on `json=...`.
However, setting a specialized JSON media type is not supported via this path, e.g. `application/custom+json; my-parameter`.

It is possible to work around this today by using `body=...` and avoiding `json=...` entirely, but this violates the principle of least-surprise. One would expect a valid Content-Type to come out of the combination of `json=..., headers=...`.

### Version of `responses`

0.23.1

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import requests
import responses

responses.add(
    responses.GET,
    "https://example.org/",
    json={},
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
)
responses.start()

r = requests.get("https://example.org/")
print(r.headers.get("Content-Type"))  # "application/json, application/json"
```

This happens with any Content-Type value, not only the JSON one. e.g. Setting `Content-Type: foo` results in `application/json, foo`.

### Expected Result

Content-Type should only ever have a single value, although some HTTP client implementations attempt to parse it as a list for broader compatibility with malformed data. ([Relevant section of RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#field.content-type).)

There are various behaviors which could be chosen here. e.g. Any match for `application/.*\+json;.*` could be used as a replacement, but headers could be otherwise concatenated.

However, the least surprising behavior would be for the explicit `Content-Type` header to _always_ override the implicit one from `json=...`.

### Actual Result

Content-Type header values are comma-joined, producing a header which does not consistently parse as JSON depending on the mimetype detection algorithm used.

    48	* Plenty of predefined *styles* for multiple use cases and option to

    19	```

<issue_description>
WsgiToAsgi should stop sending response body after content-length bytes
Hi,

I was having issues when serving partial requests (using Range headers) from [whitenoise](https://github.com/evansd/whitenoise) wrapped in WsgiToAsgi. Some HTTP and ASGI servers in front of that complained about extra content in the response body (I've had the issue with traefik in front of uvicorn and with [uvicorn itself when using the httptools protocol handler](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/master/uvicorn/protocols/http/httptools_impl.py#L517)).

One contributing factor is whitenoise which returns the file handle to the whole file in a [wsgiref.FileWrapper](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/master/Lib/wsgiref/util.py#L11), seeked to the correct position for the range request. It then expects the server to only read as many bytes as defined in the Content-Length header.

The [WSGI specs allows for this behavior](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3333/#handling-the-content-length-header) and [gunicorn implements it](https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/blob/master/gunicorn/http/wsgi.py#L333) and stops reading after as many bytes as specified in Content-Length.

The [ASGI spec](https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/specs/www.html#http) does not say much about the consistency between Content-Length header and the "http.response.body" events. The relevant parts could be :
> Protocol servers must flush any data passed to them into the send buffer before returning from a send call.

> Yielding content from the WSGI application maps to sending http.response.body messages.

The first one suggests that any piece of body from an "http.response.body" event must be sent, the other one could mean that all behavior defined for WSGI should apply to ASGI, including not-sending extra body, maybe ?

[uvicorn](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/master/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L475), [daphe](https://github.com/django/daphne/blob/master/daphne/http_protocol.py#L255) and [hypercorn](https://gitlab.com/pgjones/hypercorn/-/blob/master/src/hypercorn/protocol/http_stream.py#L147) lean more towards the first interpretation and pass through the whole readable content or simply raise an exception.

If you agree that the WsgiToAsgi adapter should clamp the body I can work on a patch.

Aside from this, the ASGI spec could probably be improved by defining this point. I don't really know if ASGI servers should prefer clamping or forwarding extra body responses but I have the vague feeling that allowing ASGI events to generate incorrectly framed HTTP messages could generate hard to diagnose issues in the future without providing any benefit.

If the sendfile extension from #184 is added, the same point will probably arise, it would be very inconvenient to only be able to use sendfile when serving whole files. WSGI also specifies the clamping behavior [when using sendfile](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3333/#optional-platform-specific-file-handling) and [gunicorn](https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/blob/master/gunicorn/http/wsgi.py#L365) implements it.

### 1.1-1.5 Problem Analysis

**Problem Statement**: 
- Currently, when a client sends a HELO or EHLO command twice, the server rejects it with error code `503 Duplicate HELO/EHLO`
- According to the SMTP standard, duplicate HELO/EHLO should be treated as an implicit RSET (reset) command instead of being rejected
- The current behavior contradicts the RFC standards and differs from how most other SMTP servers behave

**Technical Details**:
- File: `/workspace/aio-libs__aiosmtpd__1.0/aiosmtpd/smtp.py`
- Methods: `smtp_HELO()` (line 283) and `smtp_EHLO()` (line 299)

- Both methods already call `self._set_rset_state()` on successful execution (lines 291 and 308)

**Steps to Reproduce**:
1. Start an aiosmtpd server
2. Connect with an SMTP client
3. Send HELO or EHLO command successfully
4. Send the same HELO or EHLO command again
5. Server responds with `503 Duplicate HELO/EHLO` instead of treating it as RSET

**Best Practices for Fix**:
- Follow SMTP RFC standards
- Maintain backward compatibility where possible
- Handle both HELO and EHLO consistently
- Preserve existing session reset behavior

     4	A generic AST to represent Python2 and Python3's Abstract Syntax Tree(AST).

    97	## Public API
    98	
    99	### `ItemAdapter` class
   100	
   101	_class `itemadapter.adapter.ItemAdapter(item: Any)`_
   102	
   103	`ItemAdapter` implements the
   104	[`MutableMapping` interface](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.MutableMapping),
   105	providing a `dict`-like API to manipulate data for the object it wraps
   106	(which is modified in-place).
   107	
   108	Two additional methods are available:
   109	
   110	`get_field_meta(field_name: str) -> MappingProxyType`

   113	object, which is a read-only mapping with metadata about the given field. If the item class does not
   114	support field metadata, or there is no metadata for the given field, an empty object is returned.
   115	
   116	The returned value is taken from the following sources, depending on the item type:
   117	
   118	* [`scrapy.item.Field`](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/latest/topics/items.html#item-fields)
   119	for `scrapy.item.Item`s

   121	  for `dataclass`-based items
   122	* [`attr.Attribute.metadata`](https://www.attrs.org/en/stable/examples.html#metadata)
   123	  for `attrs`-based items
   124	
   125	`field_names() -> List[str]`
   126	
   127	Return a list with the names of all the defined fields for the item.

   140	arbitrary field metadata, which can be retrieved with the

if field_name in adapter.field_names():  # This is O(N) - linear search through list

    85	
    86	`reach` has many options for saving and loading files, including custom separators, custom number of dimensions, loading a custom wordlist, custom number of words, and error recovery.     92	| System | Time (7 loops)    |
    93	|--------|-------------------|
    94	| Gensim | 3min 57s ± 344 ms |
    95	| reach  | 2min 14s ± 4.09 s |

    97	## Fast format
    98	
    99	`reach` has a special fast format, which is useful if you want to reload your word vectors often. The fast format can be created using the `save_fast_format` function, and loaded using the `load_fast_format` function. This is about equivalent to saving word vectors in `gensim`'s own format in terms of loading speed.
   100	
   101	# autoreach
   102	
   103	Reach also has a way of automatically inferring words from strings without using a pre-defined tokenizer, i.e., without splitting the string into words. This is useful because there might be mismatches between the tokenizer you happen to have on hand, and the word vectors you use. For example, if your vector space contains an embedding for the word `"it's"`, and your tokenizer splits this string into two tokens: `["it", "'s"]`, the embedding for `"it's"` will never be found.
   104	
   105	autoreach solves this problem by only finding words from your pre-defined vocabulary in a string, this removing the need for any tokenization. We use the [aho-corasick algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aho%E2%80%93Corasick_algorithm), which allows us to find substrings in linear time. The downside of using aho-corasick is that it also finds substrings of regular words. For example, the word `the` will be found as a substring of `these`. To circumvent this, we perform a regex-based clean-up step.
   106	
   107	**Warning! The clean-up step involves checking for surrounding spaces and punctuation marks. Hence, if the language for which you use Reach does not actually use spaces and/or punctuation marks to designate word boundaries, the entire process might not work.**
   108	
   109	### Example
   110	
   111	```python
   112	import numpy as np
   113	
   114	from reach import AutoReach
   115	
   116	words = ["dog", "walked", "home"]
   117	vectors = np.random.randn(3, 32)
   118	
   119	r = AutoReach(vectors, words)
   120	
   121	sentence = "The dog, walked, home"
   122	bow = r.bow(sentence)
   123	
   124	found_words = [r.indices[index] for index in bow]
   125	```
   126	
   127	### benchmark
   128	
   129	Because we no longer need to tokenize, `AutoReach` can be many times faster. In this benchmark, we compare to just splitting, and `nltk`'s `word_tokenize` function.
   130	
   131	We will use the entirety of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, which you can find [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/42324/pg42324.txt), and the glove.6b.50d vectors, which you can find [here](https://nlp.stanford.edu/data/glove.6B.zip).
   132	
   133	```python
   134	from pathlib import Path
   135	
   136	from nltk import word_tokenize
   137	
   138	from reach import AutoReach, Reach
   139	
   140	
   141	txt = Path("pg42324.txt").read_text().lower()
   142	normal_reach = Reach.load("glove.6B.100d.txt")
   143	auto_reach = AutoReach.load("glove.6B.100d.txt")
   144	
   145	# Ipython magic commands
   146	%timeit normal_reach.vectorize(word_tokenize(txt), remove_oov=True)
   147	# 345 ms ± 3.42 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
   148	%timeit normal_reach.vectorize(txt.split(), remove_oov=True)
   149	# 25.4 ms ± 132 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
   150	%timeit auto_reach.vectorize(txt)
   151	# 69.9 ms ± 237 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
   152	
   153	```
   154	
   155	As you can see, the tokenizer introduces significant overhead compared to just splitting, while using the aho-corasick algorithm to split is still reasonably fast.

<issue_description>
CompoundPredicate should escape `:` to avoid wrong block_keys
I've found an issue on `CompoundPredicate` caused by the lack of escaping `:` chars inside fields.

This causes two problems. First, it can generate duplicate `block_key`s for the same `id`. Here's the example:

```
(SimplePredicate: (commonSetElementPredicate, name), SimplePredicate: (commonSetElementPredicate, address))
```

```
id  | name            | address    
---------------------------------------
1   | {'foo:', 'foo'} | {':bar', 'bar'}
```

```
id | block_key
---------------
1  | foo::bar:0
1  | foo::bar:0
```

That's probably not problematic for Dedupe 2, but that breaks [this line](https://github.com/dedupeio/dedupe-examples/blob/83dbf872674a5c3f6a209c367f46c7e6ef78e9a3/pgsql_big_dedupe_example/pgsql_big_dedupe_example.py#L246-L247) of the old `smaller_id`-based big Dedupe I still use.

Second, it can group together under the same `block_key` records that shouldn't be blocked together. See:

```
(SimplePredicate: (wholeFieldPredicate, name), SimplePredicate: (wholeFieldPredicate, address))
```

```
id  | name    | address    
---------------------------
1   | flavio: | one street
2   | flavio  | :one street
```

```
id | blocking_key
-------------------------
1  | flavio::one street:0
2  | flavio::one street:0
```

The solution is to escape `:` right before performing the `join` at this line:

https://github.com/dedupeio/dedupe/blob/5092f2598f1f2bcb4f3b1f0ec85f88b95ce7454b/dedupe/predicates.py#L332

Something like `u':'.join(block_key.replace(u':', u'\\:'))` would work, because the examples above would become this:

```
id | block_key
---------------
1  | foo\::bar:0
1  | foo:\:bar:0
```

```
id | blocking_key
-------------------------
1  | flavio\::one street:0
2  | flavio:\:one street:0
```

I'll open a PR for this.
