    20	Hist is a analyst friendly front-end for
    21	[boost-histogram](https://github.com/scikit-hep/boost-histogram), designed for
    22	Python 3.6+. See [what's new](https://hist.readthedocs.io/en/latest/changelog.html).
    23	
    24	## Installation
    25	
    26	You can install this library from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/hist/) with pip:
    27	
    28	```bash
    29	python3 -m pip install "hist[plot]"
    30	```
    31	
    32	If you do not need the plotting features, you can skip the `[plot]` extra.
    33	
    34	## Features
    35	
    36	Hist currently provides everything boost-histogram provides, and the following enhancements:
    37	
    38	- Hist augments axes with names:
    39	  - `name=` is a unique label describing each axis.
    40	  - `label=` is an optional string that is used in plotting (defaults to `name`
    41	    if not provided).
    42	  - Indexing, projection, and more support named axes.
    43	  - Experimental `NamedHist` is a `Hist` that disables most forms of positional access.
    44	
    45	- The `Hist` class augments `bh.Histogram` with reduced typing construction:
    46	  - Optional import-free construction system
    47	  - `flow=False` is a fast way to turn off flow
    48	  - Storages can be given by string
    49	  - `storage=` can be omitted
    50	  - `data=` can initialize a histogram with existing data
    51	  - `Hist.from_columns` can be used to initialize with a DataFrame or dict
    52	
    53	- Hist implements UHI+; an extension to the UHI (Unified Histogram Indexing) system designed for import-free interactivity:
    54	  - Uses `j` suffix to switch to data coordinates in access or slices
    55	  - Uses `j` suffix on slices to rebin
    56	  - Strings can be used directly to index into string category axes
    57	
    58	- Quick plotting routines encourage exploration:
    59	  - `.plot()` provides 1D and 2D plots
    60	  - `.plot2d_full()` shows 1D projects around a 2D plot
    61	  - `.plot_pull(...)` performs a pull plot
    62	  - `.plot_pie()` makes a pie plot
    63	
    64	- Notebook ready: Hist has gorgeous in-notebook representation.
    65	  - No dependencies required
    66	
    67	## Usage
    68	
    69	```python
    70	from hist import Hist
    71	
    72	# Quick construction, no other imports needed:
    73	h = (
    74	  Hist.new
    75	  .Reg(10, 0 ,1, name="x", label="x-axis")
    76	  .Var(range(10), name="y", label="y-axis")
    77	  .Int64()
    78	)
    79	
    80	# Filling by names is allowed:
    81	h.fill(y=[1, 4, 6], x=[3, 5, 2])
    82	
    83	# Names can be used to manipulate the histogram:
    84	h.project("x")
    85	h[{"y": 0.5j + 3, "x": 5j}]
    86	
    87	# You can access data coordinates or rebin with a `j` suffix:
    88	h[.3j:, ::2j] # x from .3 to the end, y is rebinned by 2
    89	
    90	# Elegant plotting functions:
    91	h.plot()
    92	h.plot2d_full()
    93	h.plot_pull(Callable)
    94	```

    94	model (and therefore have an effect on the cost minimization). But while they are only used to control the system and
    95	are no real costs, they are not used in the financial evaluation at the end of the simulation.
    96	
    97	### Foreign States
    98	Some components behaviour is dependant on so called foreign states, that is a state or attribute of another component
    99	(e.g. the artificial costs of the electricity grid can be dependant on a storage state of charge in order to fill
   100	the storage with grid electricity when the storage is below a certain threshold). While the effect of the foreign states
   101	is determined in the component itself, the mechanics on how to define the foreign states is the same for each component.
   102	Foreign states are always defined by the attributes:
   103	* fs_component_name: String (or list of strings for multiple foreign states) of the foreign component.
   104	* fs_attribute_name: String (or list of strings for multiple foreign states) of the attribute name of the component.
   105	
   106	If a fixed value should be used as a foreign state, here fs_component_name has to be set to None and fs_attribute_name
   107	has to be set to the numeric value.
   108	
   109	## Financials
   110	The costs and revenues are tracked for each component individually. They can be divided in variable costs and
   111	CAPEX and OPEX. The variable costs are costs that depend on the operation of a component, for example the
   112	amount of electricity a grid supplies. The CAPEX and OPEX are defined by the model parameters. CAPEX are
   113	one time investment costs (in EUR) and OPEX are annual operation costs (in EUR/a).
   114	
   115	After the simulation, all costs and revenues are transferred to annuities (yearly costs in EUR/a). This way,
   116	the costs can be mixed together and different models of different simulations times can be compared.
   117	
   118	### Variable Costs
   119	Variable costs are costs that are dependant on the operation of a component (e.g. fuel or electricity costs).
   120	
   121	### CAPEX and OPEX
   122	Next to variable costs, each component can have one time investment costs (CAPEX) and annual operation
   123	costs (OPEX). Those costs can be set by the parameters "opex" and "capex", both being dictionaries.
   124	Both dictionaries can have the following key values:
   125	
   126	* *cost*: can be set directly with key set to "fix", otherwise the cost are calculated dependant on
   127	    *dependant_value*
   128	* *key*: defines how the costs should be calculated, a description in more detail can be found below
   129	* *dependant_value*: string of the component parameter the cost value depends on
   130	* *fitting_value*: for the keys "exp", "poly" and "free" fitting values are needed to calculate the costs
   131	
   132	After the calculations, the units of CAPEX are always EUR and the unit of OPEX are always EUR/a.
   133	
   134	#### Fitting Methods
   135	The fitting method of the cost is chosen by the key. The different fitting methods are:
   136	* fix: No fitting is done, the value given as *cost*. The *cost* value for CAPEX is taken in EUR while the
   137	    cost value for OPEX is taken in EUR/a.
   138	    ```
   139	    cost = cost
   140	    ```
   141	* spec: Specific cost that are dependant on one component parameter (e.g. EUR/kW) are given. The value of
   142	*dependant_value* is a string of the parameter name (e.g. "power_max"). *fitting_value* is multiplied with
   143	    the value of the parameter to get the costs:
   144	    ```
   145	    cost = fitting_value * component[dependant_value]
   146	    ```
   147	    As one special case, as *dependant_value* for the OPEX calculation, "capex" can be choosen. In that case,
   148	    the fitting value is multiplied with the CAPEX, which are calculated before the OPEX (as an example, if
   149	    *dependant_value* = "capex" and *fitting_value* = 0.04, the OPEX will be 4 % of the CAPEX in EUR/a).
   150	
   151	    Another special case is choosing "cost" as *fitting_value*, that way the current cost value is used as
   152	    fitting value.
   153	* exp: Exponential fitting of the costs. A list of two or three entries can be given as *fitting_value*, the
   154	    costs are calculated in the following way:
   155	    ```
   156	    for two fitting values [fv_1, fv_2]:
   157	    cost = fv_1 * exp(dependant_value * fv_2)
   158	
   159	    for three fitting values [fv_1, fv_2, fv_3]:
   160	    cost = fv_1 + fv_2 * exp(dependant_value * fv_3)
   161	    ```
   162	* poly: Polynomial fitting, where an arbitrary amount of fitting values can be given as a lig. The costs are
   163	    calculated like:
   164	    ```
   165	    for an arbitrary number of fitting values [fv_1, fv_2, fv_3, ..., fv_n]
   166	    cost = fv_1 + fv_2 * dependant_value**1 + fv_3 * dependant_value**2 + ... + fv_n * dependant_value**(n-1)
   167	    ```
   168	* free: Like the polynomial fitting, but here the exponents can be chosen freely. As *fitting_values*, a list
   169	    with an even number of fitting values has to be given. The costs are calculated like:
   170	    ```
   171	    for an even number of fitting values [fv_1, fv_2, fv_3, ..., fv_n]
   172	    cost = fv_1 * dependant_value**fv_2 + fv_3 * dependant_value**fv_4 + ... + fv_(n-1) * dependant_value**fv_n
   173	    ```
   174	
   175	### Financial Results
   176	In order to make the variable costs, CAPEX and OPEX comparable, once the simulation is done, annuities are
   177	calculated. To get an annuity, the following steps have to be done:
   178	
   179	* variable costs: The variable costs of one component are summed up and represent the costs or revenues generated
   180	in the simulation period. To get a yearly payment or revenue, the values for simulation times other than one year
   181	have to be corrected by that time.
   182	    ```
   183	    var_cost_annuity = sum(var_cost) * 365_days / simulated_days
   184	    ```
   185	* CAPEX: To derive an annuity, the one time investment or CAPEX have to be transferred by taking into account the
   186	life time (lt) of the component and the interest rate (ir). The equation is shown in the following:
   187	    ```
   188	    capex_annuity = capex * (ir * (1 + ir)**lt) / (((1 + ir)**lt) - 1)
   189	    ```
   190	* OPEX: The OPEX are already yearly costs and don't have to be transformed.
   191

2 3 [![Build Status][build-badge]][travis] 4 [![Coverage Status][cover-badge]][coveralls] 5 [![PyPI][pypi-badge]][pypi] 6 [![is wheel][wheel-badge]][pypi] 7 8 mistletoe is a Markdown parser in pure Python, 9 designed to be fast, spec-compliant and fully customizable. 10 11 Apart from being the fastest 12 CommonMark-compliant Markdown parser implementation in pure Python, 13 mistletoe also supports easy definitions of custom tokens. 14 Parsing Markdown into an abstract syntax tree 15 also allows us to swap out renderers for different output formats, 16 without touching any of the core components. 17 18 Remember to spell mistletoe in lowercase! 19 20 Features 21 -------- 22 * **Fast**: 23 mistletoe is the fastest implementation of CommonMark in Python, 24 that is, 2 to 3 times as fast as [Commonmark-py][commonmark-py], 25 and still roughly 30% faster than [Python-Markdown][python-markdown]. 26 Running with PyPy yields comparable performance with [mistune][mistune]. 27 28 See the [performance](#performance) section for details. 29 30 * **Spec-compliant**: 31 CommonMark is [a useful, high-quality project][oilshell]. 32 mistletoe follows the [CommonMark specification][commonmark] 33 to resolve ambiguities during parsing. 34 Outputs are predictable and well-defined. 35 36 * **Extensible**: 37 Strikethrough and tables are supported natively, 38 and custom block-level and span-level tokens can easily be added. 39 Writing a new renderer for mistletoe is a relatively 40 trivial task. 41 42 You can even write [a Lisp][scheme] in it. 43 44 Some alternative output formats: 45 46 * HTML 47 * LaTeX 48 * Jira Markdown ([contrib][contrib]) 49 * Mathjax ([contrib][contrib]) 50 * Scheme ([contrib][contrib]) 51 * HTML + code highlighting ([contrib][contrib]) 52 53 Installation 54 ------------ 55 mistletoe is tested for Python 3.3 and above. The function also accepts an additional argument 88 `renderer`. To produce LaTeX output: 89 90 ```python 91 import mistletoe 92 from mistletoe.latex_renderer import LaTeXRenderer 93 94 with open('foo.md', 'r') as fin: 95 rendered = mistletoe.markdown(fin, LaTeXRenderer) 96 ``` 97 98 Finally, here's how you would manually specify extra tokens and a renderer 99 for mistletoe. In the following example, we use `HTMLRenderer` to render 100 the AST, which adds `HTMLBlock` and `HTMLSpan` to the normal parsing 101 process. 102 103 ```python 104 from mistletoe import Document, HTMLRenderer 105 106 with open('foo.md', 'r') as fin: 107 with HTMLRenderer() as renderer: 108 rendered = renderer.render(Document(fin)) 109 ``` 110 111 ### From the command-line 112 113 pip installation enables mistletoe's command-line utility. Type the following 114 directly into your shell: 115 116 ```sh 117 mistletoe foo.md 118 ``` 119 120 This will transpile `foo.md` into HTML, and dump the output to stdout. To save 121 the HTML, direct the output into a file: 122 123 ```sh 124 mistletoe foo.md > out.html 125 ``` 126 127 You can pass in custom renderers by including the full path to your renderer 128 class after a `-r` or `--renderer` flag: 129 130 ```sh 131 mistletoe foo.md --renderer custom_renderer.CustomRenderer 132 ``` 133 134 Running `mistletoe` without specifying a file will land you in interactive 135 mode. Like Python's REPL, interactive mode allows you to test how your 136 Markdown will be interpreted by mistletoe: 137 138 ```html 139 mistletoe [version 0.7.1] (interactive) 140 Type Ctrl-D to complete input, or Ctrl-C to exit. 141 >>> some **bold** text 142 ... and some *italics* 143 ... 144

foo bar

206 ``` 207 208 ... and it is indeed the output of Python-Markdown, Commonmark-py and mistletoe. 209 Mistune (version 0.8.3) greedily parses the first two asterisks 210 in the first delimiter run as a strong-emphasis opener, 211 the second delimiter run as its closer, 212 but does not know what to do with the remaining asterisk in between: 213 214 ```html 215

*foo bar*

216 ``` 217 218 The implication of this runs deeper, 219 and it is not simply a matter of dogmatically following an external spec. 220 By adopting a more flexible parsing algorithm, 221 mistletoe allows us to specify a precedence level to each token class, 222 including custom ones that you might write in the future. 223 Code spans, for example, has a higher precedence level than emphasis, 224 so 225 226 ```markdown 227 *foo `bar* baz` 228 ``` 229 230 ... is parsed as: 231 232 ```html 233

*foo bar* baz

234 ``` 235 236 ... whereas Mistune parses this as: 237 238 ```html 239

foo `bar baz`

240 ``` 241 242 Of course, it is not *impossible* for Mistune to modify its behavior, 243 and parse these two examples correctly, 244 through more sophisticated regexes or some other means. 245 It is nevertheless *highly likely* that, 246 when Mistune implements all the necessary context checks, 247 it will suffer from the same performance penalties. 248 249 Contextual analysis is why Python-Markdown is slow, and why CommonMark-py is slower. 250 The lack thereof is the reason mistune enjoys stellar performance 251 among similar parser implementations, 252 as well as the limitations that come with these performance benefits. 253 254 If you want an implementation that focuses on raw speed, 255 mistune remains a solid choice. 256 If you need a spec-compliant and readily extensible implementation, however, 257 mistletoe is still marginally faster than Python-Markdown, 258 while supporting more functionality (lists in block quotes, for example), 259 and significantly faster than CommonMark-py. 260 261 262 One last note: another bottleneck of mistletoe compared to mistune 263 is the function overhead. Because, unlike mistune, mistletoe chooses to split 264 functionality into modules, function lookups can take significantly longer than 265 mistune. To boost the performance further, it is suggested to use PyPy with mistletoe. 266 Benchmark results show that on PyPy, mistletoe's performance is on par with mistune: 267 268 ```sh 269 $ pypy3 test/benchmark.py mistune mistletoe 270 Test document: test/samples/syntax.md 271 Test iterations: 1000 272 Running tests with mistune, mistletoe... 273 ======================================== 274 mistune: 13.645681533998868 275 mistletoe: 15.088351159000013 276 ``` 277 278 Developer's Guide 279 ----------------- 280 Here's an example to add GitHub-style wiki links to the parsing process, 281 and provide a renderer for this new token. 282 283 ### A new token 284 285 GitHub wiki links are span-level tokens, meaning that they reside inline, 286 and don't really look like chunky paragraphs. import numba
import trio

async def _run():
    T = .000015
    t_start = trio.current_time()

    while True:
        t0 = trio.current_time()
        await trio.sleep(T)
        delta = trio.current_time() - t0
        if delta > .005:
            elapsed = trio.current_time() - t_start
            print(f'{(elapsed) // 60:02.0f}:{elapsed % 60:02.0f}  {delta * 1000:5.1f}')

trio.run(_run)
```

    48	### Endian-ness
    49	
    50	We use the convention that the LSB is sent out first and read in first.
    51	The location of the LSB in arrays and lists changes from object to
    52	object based on the conventions of the other packages we interact with.
    53	
    54	In particular, pyserial sends out index 0 first, so for `bytes` objects,
    55	index 0 will generally have the LSB. On the other hand, bitstrings
    56	treats the _last_ index as the LSB, which is also how numbers are
    57	usually displayed on screen, e.g. `0100` in binary means 4 not 2. So for
    58	`BitArray` and `Bits` objects, the LSB will generally be last.
    59	
    60	Note that this combination leads to the slightly awkward convention that
    61	the least significant bit of a bytestring is the *last bit* of the
    62	*first byte*. For example, if bits[15:0] of a packet are
    63	`0000 0010 0000 0001` ( = 0x0201 = 513), then the bytes will be sent out as
    64	`b'\x01\x02'`.
    65	
    66	### Creating a LArPix Chip
    67	
    68	The `Chip` object represents a single LArPix chip and knows about
    69	everything happening on the chip regarding configuration, data sent in,
    70	and data read out. To create a Chip, just provide the chip ID number
    71	(hard-wired into the PCB) and the index for the IO Chain (daisy chain)
    72	that the chip is part of:
    73	
    74	```python
    75	myChip = Chip(100, 0)
    76	```
    77	
    78	The Chip object uses these ID values when it creates data packets to
    79	ensure that the packet reaches the correct chip. And other objects use
    80	the ID values to ensure that received data from the physical chip makes
    81	its way to the right Chip object.
    82	
    83	The chip's configuration register is represented by the `myChip.config`
    84	attribute, which is an instance of the `Configuration` object.
    85	
    86	### The Configuration object
    87	
    88	The `Configuration` object represents all of the options in the LArPix
    89	configuration register. Each row in the configuration table in the LArPix datasheet
    90	has a corresponding attribute in the `Configuration` object. Per-channel
    91	attributes are stored in a list, and all other attributes are stored as
    92	a simple integer. (This includes everything from single bits to values
    93	such as "reset cycles," which spans 3 bytes.) **Warning**: there is
    94	currently no type checking or range checking on these values. Using
    95	values outside the expected range will lead to undefined behavior,
    96	including the possibility that Python will crash _or_ that LArPix will
    97	be sent bad commands.
    98	
    99	`Configuration` objects also have some helper methods for enabling and
   100	disabling per-channel settings (such as `csa_testpulse_enable` or
   101	`channel_mask`). The relevant methods are listed here and should be
   102	prefixed with either `enable_` or `disable_`:
   103	
   104	 - `channels` enables/disables the `channel_mask` register
   105	 - `external_trigger` enables/disables the `external_trigger_mask`
   106	    register
   107	 - `testpulse` enables/disables the `csa_testpulse_enable` register
   108	 - `analog_monitor` enables/disables the `csa_monitor_select` register
   109	
   110	Most of these methods accept an optional list of channels to enable or
   111	disable (and with no list specified acts on all channels). The exception
   112	is `enable_analog_monitor` (and its `disable` counterpart): the `enable`
   113	method requires a particular channel to be specified, and the `disable`
   114	method does not require any argument at all. This is because at most one
   115	channel is allowed to have the analog monitor enabled.
   116	
   117	The machinery of the `Configuration` object ensures that each value is
   118	converted to the appropriate set of bits when it comes time to send
   119	actual commands to the physical chip. Although this is not transparent
   120	to you as a user of this library, you might want to know that two sets of
   121	configuration options are always sent together in the same configuration
   122	packet:
   123	
   124	 - `csa_gain`, `csa_bypass`, and `internal_bypass` are combined into a
   125	   single byte, so even though they have their own attributes, they must
   126	   be written to the physical chip together
   127	
   128	 - `test_mode`, `cross_trigger_mode`, `periodic_reset`, and
   129	   `fifo_diagnostic` work the same way
   130	
   131	Similarly, all of the per-channel options (except for the pixel trim
   132	thresholds) are sent in 4 groups of 8 channels.
   133	
   134	Configurations can be loaded by importing `larpix.configs` and running
   135	the `load` function. This function searches for a configuration with the
   136	given filename relative to the current directory before searching the
   137	"system" location (secretly it's in the larpix/configs/ folder). This is
   138	similar to `#include "header.h"` behavior in C.
   139	
   140	Configurations can be saved by calling `chip.config.write` with the
   141	desired filename.
   142	
   143	Once the Chip object has been configured, the configuration must be sent
   144	to the physical chip. This is accomplished with the `Controller` object,
   145	which we'll discuss next.
   146	
   147	### Communicating with the physical LArPix chip
   148	
   149	Communication between the computer and the physical LArPix chip is
   150	handled by the `Controller` object and uses a Serial interface. (The
   151	interface specification is given in the fpga\_interface.txt file. It's
   152	based on RS-232 8N1.) To initialize a Controller object, simply provide
   153	the port you'd like to communicate over. For the envisioned normal
   154	application (with an FTDI chip as USB-serial bridge), this will likely
   155	be something like `/dev/ttyUSB0`.
   156	
   157	```python
   158	controller = Controller('/dev/ttyUSB0')
   159	```
   160	
   161	An important attribute of the Controller object is `chips`, which is a
   162	list of Chip objects controlled by the particular Controller. Add a
   163	single Chip object to the list with `controller.chips.append(myChip)`,
   164	or add a whole list with `controller.chips.extend(list_of_chips)`.
   165	
   166	You might want to change the following
   167	attributes at some point, but their defaults should work in most cases:

   174	   bytes to send with a single write command. The limit is entirely due

   177	#### Sending data
   178	
   179	The only data that LArPix can receive is configuration data. To send all
   180	of the configuration packets in write mode, simply call
   181	
   182	```python

   184	# Edit the configuration

Para una versión más detallada de los comportamientos, revise la [documentación oficial](http://pydatajson.readthedocs.io) o el [Manual de Uso](docs/MANUAL.md) de la librería.
    38	
    39	## Instalación
    40	
    41	* **Producción:** Desde cualquier parte
    42	
    43	```bash
    44	$ pip install pydatajson
    45	```
    46	
    47	* **Desarrollo:** Clonar este repositorio, y desde su raíz, ejecutar:
    48	```bash
    49	$ pip install -e .
    50	```
    51	
    52	A partir de la versión 0.2.x (Febrero 2017), la funcionalidad del paquete se mantendrá fundamentalmente estable hasta futuro aviso. De todas maneras, si piensa utilizar esta librería en producción, le sugerimos fijar la versión que emplea en un archivo `requirements.txt`.
    53	
    54	## Usos
    55	
    56	La librería cuenta con funciones para cuatro objetivos principales:
    57	- **validación de metadatos de catálogos** y los _datasets_,
    58	- **generación de reportes** sobre el contenido y la validez de los metadatos de catálogos y _datasets_,
    59	- **transformación de archivos de metadatos** al formato estándar (JSON), y
    60	- **generación de indicadores de monitoreo de catálogos** y sus _datasets_.
    61	
    62	A continuación se proveen ejemplos de cada uno de estas acciones. Si desea analizar un flujo de trabajo más completo, refiérase a los Jupyter Notebook de [`samples/`](samples/)
    63	
    64	### Setup
    65	
    66	`DataJson` utiliza un esquema default que cumple con el perfil de metadatos recomendado en la [Guía para el uso y la publicación de metadatos (v0.1)](https://github.com/datosgobar/paquete-apertura-datos/raw/master/docs/Guia%20para%20el%20uso%20y%20la%20publicacion%20de%20metadatos%20(v0.1).pdf) del [Paquete de Apertura de Datos](https://github.com/datosgobar/paquete-apertura-datos).
    67	
    68	```python
    69	from pydatajson import DataJson
    70	
    71	dj = DataJson()
    72	```
    73	
    74	Si se desea utilizar un esquema alternativo, por favor, consulte la sección "Uso > Setup" del [manual oficial](docs/MANUAL.md), o la documentación oficial.
    75	
    76	### Validación de metadatos de catálogos
    77	
    78	- Si se desea un **resultado sencillo (V o F)** sobre la validez de la estructura del catálogo, se utilizará **`is_valid_catalog(catalog)`**.
    79	- Si se desea un **mensaje de error detallado**, se utilizará **`validate_catalog(catalog)`**.
    80	
    81	Por conveniencia, la carpeta [`tests/samples/`](tests/samples/) contiene varios ejemplos de `data.json` bien y mal formados con distintos tipos de errores.
    82	
    83	#### Archivo data.json local
    84	
    85	```python
    86	from pydatajson import DataJson
    87	
    88	dj = DataJson()
    89	catalog = "tests/samples/full_data.json"
    90	validation_result = dj.is_valid_catalog(catalog)
    91	validation_report = dj.validate_catalog(catalog)
    92	
    93	print validation_result
    94	True
    95	
    96	print validation_report
    97	{
    98	    "status": "OK",
    99	    "error": {
   100	        "catalog": {
   101	            "status": "OK",
   102	            "errors": [],
   103	            "title": "Datos Argentina"
   104	        },
   105	        "dataset": [
   106	            {
   107	                "status": "OK",
   108	                "errors": [],
   109	                "title": "Sistema de contrataciones electrónicas"
   110	            }
   111	        ]
   112	    }
   113	}
   114	```
   115	
   116	#### Otros formatos
   117	
   118	`pydatajson` puede interpretar catálogos tanto en formato JSON como en formato XLSX (siempre y cuando se hayan creado utilizando la [plantilla](samples/plantilla_data.xlsx), estén estos almacenados localmente o remotamente a través de URLs de descarga directa. También es capaz de interpretar diccionarios de Python con metadatos de catálogos.
   119	
   120	```python
   121	from pydatajson import DataJson
   122	
   123	dj = DataJson()
   124	catalogs = [
   125	    "tests/samples/full_data.json", # archivo JSON local
   126	    "http://181.209.63.71/data.json", # archivo JSON remoto
   127	    "tests/samples/catalogo_justicia.xlsx", # archivo XLSX local
   128	    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datosgobar/pydatajson/master/tests/samples/catalogo_justicia.xlsx", # archivo XLSX remoto
   129	    {
   130	        "title": "Catálogo del Portal Nacional",
   131		"description" "Datasets abiertos para el ciudadano."
   132	        "dataset": [...],
   133		(...)
   134	    } # diccionario de Python
   135	]
   136	
   137	for catalog in catalogs:
   138	    validation_result = dj.is_valid_catalog(catalog)
   139	    validation_report = dj.validate_catalog(catalog)
   140	```
   141	
   142	### Generación de reportes y configuraciones del Harvester
   143	
   144	Si ya se sabe que se desean cosechar todos los _datasets_ [válidos] de uno o varios catálogos, se pueden utilizar directamente el método `generate_harvester_config()`, proveyendo `harvest='all'` o `harvest='valid'` respectivamente. Si se desea revisar manualmente la lista de _datasets_ contenidos, se puede invocar primero `generate_datasets_report()`, editar el reporte generado y luego proveérselo a `generate_harvester_config()`, junto con la opción `harvest='report'`.
   145	
   146	#### Crear un archivo de configuración eligiendo manualmente los datasets a federar
   147	
   148	```python
   149	catalogs = ["tests/samples/full_data.json", "http://181.209.63.71/data.json"]
   150	report_path = "path/to/report.xlsx"
   151	dj.generate_datasets_report(
   152	    catalogs=catalogs,
   153	    harvest='none', # El reporte tendrá `harvest==0` para todos los datasets
   154	    export_path=report_path
   155	)
   156	
   157	# A continuación, se debe editar el archivo de Excel 'path/to/report.xlsx',
   158	# cambiando a '1' el campo 'harvest' en los datasets que se quieran cosechar.
   159	
   160	config_path = 'path/to/config.csv'
   161	dj.generate_harvester_config(
   162	    harvest='report',
   163	    report=report_path,
   164	    export_path=config_path
   165	)
   166	```
   167	El archivo `config_path` puede ser provisto a Harvester para federar los _datasets_ elegidos al editar el reporte intermedio `report_path`.
   168	
   169	Por omisión, en la salida de `generate_harvester_config` la frecuencia de actualización deseada para cada _dataset_ será "R/P1D", para intentar cosecharlos diariamente. De preferir otra frecuencia (siempre y cuando sea válida según ISO 8601), se la puede especificar a través del parámetro opcional `frequency`. Si especifica expĺicitamente `frequency=None`, se conservarán las frecuencias de actualización indicadas en el campo `accrualPeriodicity` de cada _dataset_.
   170	
   171	#### Crear un archivo de configuración que incluya únicamente los datasets con metadata válida
   172	
   173	Conservando las variables anteriores:
   174	
   175	```python
   176	dj.generate_harvester_config(
   177	    catalogs=catalogs,
   178	    harvest='valid'
   179	    export_path='path/to/config.csv'
   180	)
   181	```
   182	
   183	### Transformación de un archivo de metados XLSX al estándar JSON
   184	
   185	```python
   186	from pydatajson.readers import read_catalog
   187	from pydatajson.writers import write_json
   188	from pydatajson import DataJson
   189	
   190	dj = DataJson()
   191	catalogo_xlsx = "tests/samples/catalogo_justicia.xlsx"
   192	
   193	catalogo = read_catalog(catalogo_xlsx)
   194	write_json(obj=catalogo, path="tests/temp/catalogo_justicia.json")
   195	```
   196	
   197	### Generación de indicadores de monitoreo de catálogos
   198	
   199	`pydatajson` puede calcular indicadores sobre uno o más catálogos. Estos indicadores recopilan información de interés sobre los _datasets_ de cada uno, tales como:
   200	- el estado de validez de los catálogos;
   201	- el número de días desde su última actualización;
   202	- el formato de sus distribuciones;
   203	- frecuencia de actualización de los _datasets_;
   204	- estado de federación de los _datasets_, comparándolo con el catálogo central
   205	
   206	La función usada es `generate_catalogs_indicators`, que acepta los catálogos como parámetros. Devuelve dos valores:
   207	- una lista con tantos valores como catálogos, con cada elemento siendo un diccionario con los indicadores del catálogo respectivo;
   208	- un diccionario con los indicadores de la red entera (una suma de los individuales)
   209	
   210	```python
   211	catalogs = ["tests/samples/full_data.json", "http://181.209.63.71/data.json"]
   212	indicators, network_indicators = dj.generate_catalogs_indicators(catalogs)
   213	
   214	# Opcionalmente podemos pasar como segundo argumento un catálogo central,
   215	# para poder calcular indicadores sobre la federación de los datasets en 'catalogs'
   216	
   217	central_catalog = "http://datos.gob.ar/data.json"
   218	indicators, network_indicators = dj.generate_catalogs_indicators(catalogs, central_catalog)
   219	```
   220	
   221	## Tests
   222	
   223	Los tests se corren con `nose`. Desde la raíz del repositorio:
   224	
   225	**Configuración inicial:**
   226	
   227	```bash
   228	$ pip install -r requirements_dev.txt
   229	$ mkdir tests/temp
   230	```
   231	
   232	**Correr la suite de tests:**
   233	
   234	```bash
   235	$ nosetests
   236	```
   237	
   238	## Recursos de interés
   239	
   240	* [Estándar ISO 8601 - Wikipedia](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601)
   241	* [JSON SChema - Sitio oficial del estándar](http://json-schema.org/)
   242	* [Documentación completa de `pydatajson` - Read the Docs](http://pydatajson.readthedocs.io)
   243	* [Guía para el uso y la publicación de metafatos](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Z7XhpzOinvITN_9wqUbOYpceDzic3KTOHLtHcGCPAwo/edit)
   244	
   245	## Créditos
   246	
   247	El validador de archivos `data.json` desarrollado es mayormente un envoltorio (*wrapper*) alrededor de la librería [`jsonschema`](https://github.com/Julian/jsonschema), que implementa el vocabulario definido por [JSONSchema.org](http://json-schema.org/) para anotar y validar archivos JSON.

     7	## What is submitit?
     8	
     9	Submitit is a lightweight tool for submitting Python functions for computation within a Slurm cluster.
    10	It basically wraps submission and provide access to results, logs and more.
    11	[Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/quickstart.html) is an open source, fault-tolerant, and highly scalable cluster management and job scheduling system for large and small Linux clusters.

    14	### An example is worth a thousand words: performing an addition
    15	
    16	From inside an environment with `submitit` installed:
    17	
    18	```python
    19	import submitit
    20	
    21	def add(a, b):
    22	    return a + b
    23	
    24	# executor is the submission interface (logs are dumped in the folder)
    25	executor = submitit.AutoExecutor(folder="log_test")
    26	# set timeout in min, and partition for running the job
    27	executor.update_parameters(timeout_min=1, slurm_partition="dev")
    28	job = executor.submit(add, 5, 7)  # will compute add(5, 7)
    29	print(job.job_id)  # ID of your job
    30	
    31	output = job.result()  # waits for completion and returns output
    32	assert output == 12  # 5 + 7 = 12...  your addition was computed in the cluster
    33	```
    34

    38	By default stdout is silenced in `CommandFunction`, but it can be unsilenced with `verbose=True`.

    76	### Goals
    77	
    78	The aim of this Python3 package is to be able to launch jobs on Slurm painlessly from *inside Python*, using the same submission and job patterns than the standard library package `concurrent.futures`:
    79	
    80	Here are a few benefits of using this lightweight package:
    81	 - submit any function, even lambda and script-defined functions.
    82	 - raises an error with stack trace if the job failed.
    83	 - requeue preempted jobs (Slurm only)
    84	 - swap between `submitit` executor and one of `concurrent.futures` executors in a line, so that it is easy to run your code either on slurm, or locally with multithreading for instance.
    85	 - checkpoints stateful callables when preempted or timed-out and requeue from current state (advanced feature).
    86	 - easy access to task local/global rank for multi-nodes/tasks jobs.
    87	 - same code can work for different clusters thanks to a plugin system.
    88	
    89	Submitit is used by FAIR researchers on the FAIR cluster.
    90	The defaults are chosen to make their life easier, and might not be ideal for every cluster.
    91	
    92	### Non-goals
    93	
    94	- a commandline tool for running slurm jobs. Here, everything happens inside Python. To this end, you can however use [Hydra](https://hydra.cc/)'s [submitit plugin](https://hydra.cc/docs/next/plugins/submitit_launcher) (version >= 1.0.0).
    95	- a task queue, this only implements the ability to launch tasks, but does not schedule them in any way.
    96	- being used in Python2! This is a Python3.6+ only package :)

    99	### Comparison with dask.distributed
   100	
   101	[`dask`](https://distributed.dask.org/en/latest/) is a nice framework for distributed computing. `dask.distributed` provides the same `concurrent.futures` executor API as `submitit`:
   102	
   103	```python
   104	from distributed import Client
   105	from dask_jobqueue import SLURMCluster
   106	cluster = SLURMCluster(processes=1, cores=2, memory="2GB")
   107	cluster.scale(2)  # this may take a few seconds to launch
   108	executor = Client(cluster)
   109	executor.submit(...)
   110	```
   111	
   112	The key difference with `submitit` is that `dask.distributed` distributes the jobs to a pool of workers (see the `cluster` variable above) while `submitit` jobs are directly jobs on the cluster. In that sense `submitit` is a lower level interface than `dask.distributed` and you get more direct control over your jobs, including individual `stdout` and `stderr`, and possibly checkpointing in case of preemption and timeout. On the other hand, you should avoid submitting multiple small tasks with `submitit`, which would create many independent jobs and possibly overload the cluster, while you can do it without any problem through `dask.distributed`.

The issue is about supporting **inhomogeneous uncertainties** - where different bins can have different uncertainty components. 

**Key technical details:**

- **Current workaround**: Setting uncertainty to zero, but this is semantically different from not having the component

2. First two bins have error components 'A' and 'B' (but not 'C')
3. Third bin has error component 'C' (but not 'A' and 'B')

    12	
    13	## Overview
    14	
    15	Syrupy is a [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/) snapshot plugin. It enables developers to write tests which assert immutability of computed results.
    16	
    17	## Motivation
    18	
    19	The most popular snapshot test plugin compatible with pytest has some core limitations which this package attempts to address by upholding some key values:
    20	
    21	- Extensible: If a particular data type is not supported, users should be able to easily and quickly add support.
    22	- Idiomatic: Snapshot testing should fit naturally among other test cases in pytest, e.g. `assert x == snapshot` vs. `snapshot.assert_match(x)`.
    23	- Soundness: Snapshot tests should uncover even the most minute issues. Unlike other snapshot libraries, Syrupy will fail a test suite if a snapshot does not exist, not just on snapshot differences.
    24	
    25	## Installation
    26	
    27	```shell
    28	python -m pip install syrupy
    29	```
    30	
    31	### Migration from snapshottest
    32	
    33	You cannot use syrupy alongside snapshottest due to argument conflicts. To ease migration, we've made syrupy aware of snapshottest call syntax. Simply uninstall snapshottest and remove old snapshots:
    34	
    35	```shell
    36	pip uninstall snapshottest -y;
    37	find . -type d ! -path '*/\.*' -name 'snapshots' | xargs rm -r
    38	```
    39	
    40	### Pytest and Python Compatibility
    41	
    42	Syrupy will always be compatible with the latest version of Python and Pytest. If you're running an old version of Python or Pytest, you will need to use an older major version of Syrupy:
    43	
    44	| Syrupy Version | Python Support | Pytest Support |
    45	| -------------- | -------------- | -------------- |
    46	| 4.x.x          | >3.8.1         | >=7            |
    47	| 3.x.x          | >=3.7, <4      | >=5.1, <8      |
    48	| 2.x.x          | >=3.6, <4      | >=5.1, <8      |
    49	
    50	
    51	## Usage
    52	
    53	### Basic Usage
    54	
    55	In a pytest test file `test_file.py`:
    56	
    57	```python
    58	def test_foo(snapshot):
    59	    actual = "Some computed value!"
    60	    assert actual == snapshot
    61	```
    62	
    63	when you run `pytest`, the above test should fail due to a missing snapshot. Re-run pytest with the update snapshots flag like so:
    64	
    65	```shell
    66	pytest --snapshot-update
    67	```
    68	
    69	A snapshot file should be generated under a `__snapshots__` directory in the same directory as `test_file.py`. The `__snapshots__` directory and all its children should be committed along with your test code.
    70	
    71	[![Usage Demo](https://tophat.github.io/syrupy/assets/usage_demo.gif)](https://asciinema.org/a/369462)
    72	
    73	#### Custom Objects
    74	
    75	The default serializer supports all python built-in types and provides a sensible default for custom objects.
    76	
    77	#### Representation
    78	
    79	If you need to customise your object snapshot, it is as easy as overriding the default `__repr__` implementation.
    80	
    81	```python
    82	def __repr__(self) -> str:
    83	    return "MyCustomClass(...)"
    84	```
    85	
    86	#### Attributes
    87	
    88	If you want to limit what properties are serialized at a class type level you could either:
    89	
    90	**A**. Provide a filter function to the snapshot [exclude](#exclude) configuration option.
    91	
    92	```py
    93	def limit_foo_attrs(prop, path):
    94	  allowed_foo_attrs = {"only", "serialize", "these", "attrs"}
    95	  return isinstance(path[-1][1], Foo) and prop in allowed_foo_attrs
    96	
    97	def test_bar(snapshot):
    98	    actual = Foo(...)
    99	    assert actual == snapshot(exclude=limit_foo_attrs)
   100	```
   101	
   102	**B**. Or override the `__dir__` implementation to control the attribute list.
   103	
   104	```py
   105	class Foo:
   106	  def __dir__(self):
   107	    return ["only", "serialize", "these", "attrs"]
   108	
   109	def test_bar(snapshot):
   110	    actual = Foo(...)
   111	    assert actual == snapshot
   112	```
   113	
   114	Both options will generate equivalent snapshots but the latter is only viable when you have control over the class implementation and do not need to share the exclusion logic with other objects.
   115	
   116	### CLI Options
   117	
   118	These are the cli options exposed to `pytest` by the plugin.
   119	
   120	| Option                         | Description                                                                                                                    | Default                                          |
   121	| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
   122	| `--snapshot-update`            | Snapshots will be updated to match assertions and unused snapshots will be deleted.                                            | `False`                                          |
   123	| `--snapshot-details`           | Includes details of unused snapshots (test name and snapshot location) in the final report.                                    | `False`                                          |
   124	| `--snapshot-warn-unused`       | Prints a warning on unused snapshots rather than fail the test suite.                                                          | `False`                                          |
   125	| `--snapshot-default-extension` | Use to change the default snapshot extension class.                                                                            | [AmberSnapshotExtension](https://github.com/tophat/syrupy/blob/main/src/syrupy/extensions/amber/__init__.py) |
   126	| `--snapshot-no-colors`         | Disable test results output highlighting. Equivalent to setting the environment variables `ANSI_COLORS_DISABLED` or `NO_COLOR` | Disabled by default if not in terminal.          |
   127	
   128	### Assertion Options
   129	
   130	These are the options available on the `snapshot` assertion fixture.
   131	Use of these options are one shot and do not persist across assertions.
   132	For more persistent options see [advanced usage](#advanced-usage).
   133	
   134	#### `matcher`
   135	
   136	This allows you to match on a property path and value to control how specific object shapes are serialized.
   137	
   138	The matcher is a function that takes two keyword arguments.
   139	It should return the replacement value to be serialized or the original unmutated value.
   140	
   141	| Argument | Description                                                                                                        |
   142	| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
   143	| `data`   | Current serializable value being matched on                                                                        |
   144	| `path`   | Ordered path traversed to the current value e.g. `(("a", dict), ("b", dict))` from `{ "a": { "b": { "c": 1 } } }`} |
   145	
   146	**NOTE:** Do not mutate the value received as it could cause unintended side effects.
   147	
   148	##### Built-In Matchers
   149	
   150	Syrupy comes with built-in helpers that can be used to make easy work of using property matchers.
   151	
   152	###### `path_type(mapping=None, *, types=(), strict=True, regex=False)`
   153	
   154	Easy way to build a matcher that uses the path and value type to replace serialized data.
   155	When strict, this will raise a `ValueError` if the types specified are not matched.
   156	
   157	| Argument  | Description                                                                                                                        |
   158	| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   159	| `mapping` | Dict of path string to tuples of class types, including primitives e.g. (MyClass, UUID, datetime, int, str)                        |
   160	| `types`   | Tuple of class types used if none of the path strings from the mapping are matched                                                 |
   161	| `strict`  | If a path is matched but the value at the path does not match one of the class types in the tuple then a `PathTypeError` is raised |
   162	| `regex`   | If true, the `mapping` key is treated as a regular expression when matching paths                                                  |
   163	
   164	```py
   165	from syrupy.matchers import path_type
   166	
   167	def test_bar(snapshot):
   168	    actual = {
   169	      "date_created": datetime.now(),
   170	      "value": "Some computed value!!",
   171	    }
   172	    assert actual == snapshot(matcher=path_type({
   173	      "date_created": (datetime,),
   174	      "nested.path.id": (int,),
   175	    }))
   176	```
   177	
   178	```py
   179	# name: test_bar
   180	  dict({
   181	    'date_created': datetime,
   182	    'value': 'Some computed value!!',
   183	  })
   184	# ---
   185	```
   186	
   187	#### `exclude`
   188	
   189	This allows you to filter out object properties from the serialized snapshot.
   190	
   191	The exclude parameter takes a filter function that accepts two keyword arguments.
   192	It should return `true` or `false` if the property should be excluded or included respectively.
   193	
   194	| Argument | Description                                                                                                                                   |
   195	| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   196	| `prop`   | Current property on the object, could be any hashable value that can be used to retrieve a value e.g. `1`, `"prop_str"`, `SomeHashableObject` |
   197	| `path`   | Ordered path traversed to the current value e.g. `(("a", dict), ("b", dict))` from `{ "a": { "b": { "c": 1 } } }`}                            |
   198	
   199	##### Built-In Filters
   200	
   201	Syrupy comes with built-in helpers that can be used to make easy work of using the filter options.
   202	
   203	###### `props(prop_name, *prop_name)`
   204	
   205	Easy way to build a filter that excludes based on string based property names.
   206	
   207	Takes an argument list of property names, with support for indexed iterables.
   208	
   209	```py
   210	from syrupy.filters import props
   211	
   212	def test_bar(snapshot):
   213	    actual = {
   214	      "id": uuid.uuid4(),
   215	      "list": [1,2,3],
   216	    }
   217	    assert actual == snapshot(exclude=props("id", "1"))
   218	```
   219	
   220	```py
   221	# name: test_bar
   222	  dict({
   223	    'list': list([
   224	      1,
   225	      3,
   226	    ]),
   227	  })
   228	# ---
   229	```
   230	
   231	###### `paths(path_string, *path_strings)`
   232	
   233	Easy way to build a filter that uses full path strings delimited with `.`.
   234	
   235	Takes an argument list of path strings.
   236	
   237	```py
   238	from syrupy.filters import paths
   239	
   240	def test_bar(snapshot):
   241	    actual = {
   242	      "date": datetime.now(),
   243	      "list": [1,2,3],
   244	    }
   245	    assert actual == snapshot(exclude=paths("date", "list.1"))
   246	```
   247	
   248	```py
   249	# name: test_bar
   250	  dict({
   251	    'list': list([
   252	      1,
   253	      3,
   254	    ]),
   255	  })
   256	# ---
   257	```
   258	
   259	#### `extension_class`
   260	
   261	This is a way to modify how the snapshot matches and serializes your data in a single assertion.
   262	
   263	```py
   264	def test_foo(snapshot):
   265	    actual_svg = "<svg></svg>"
   266	    assert actual_svg == snapshot(extension_class=SVGImageSnapshotExtension)
   267	```
   268	
   269	#### `diff`
   270	
   271	This is an option to snapshot only the diff between the actual object and a previous snapshot, with the `diff` argument being the previous snapshot `index`/`name`.
   272	
   273	```py
   274	def test_diff(snapshot):
   275	    actual0 = [1,2,3,4]
   276	    actual1 = [0,1,3,4]
   277	
   278	    assert actual0 == snapshot
   279	    assert actual1 == snapshot(diff=0)
   280	    # This is equivalent to the lines above
   281	    # Must use the index name to diff when given
   282	    assert actual0 == snapshot(name='snap_name')
   283	    assert actual1 == snapshot(diff='snap_name')
   284	```
   285	
   286	##### Built-In Extensions
   287	
   288	Syrupy comes with a few built-in preset configurations for you to choose from. You should also feel free to extend the `AbstractSyrupyExtension` if your project has a need not captured by one our built-ins.
   289	
   290	- **`AmberSnapshotExtension`**: This is the default extension which generates `.ambr` files. Serialization of most data types are supported.
   291	  - Line control characters are normalised when snapshots are generated i.e. `\r` and `\n` characters are all written as `\n`. This is to allow interoperability of snapshots between operating systems that use disparate line control characters.
   292	- **`SingleFileSnapshotExtension`**: Unlike the `AmberSnapshotExtension`, which groups all tests within a single test file into a singular snapshot file, this extension creates one `.raw` file per test case.
   293	- **`PNGImageSnapshotExtension`**: An extension of single file, this should be used to produce `.png` files from a byte string.
   294	- **`SVGImageSnapshotExtension`**: Another extension of single file. This produces `.svg` files from an svg string.
